chapters.title: Calcutta's Shadowed Years
paragraphs: Primal Instinct
One

Since the time of the Second World War, the value of human life in Bengal—especially in the city of Calcutta—has diminished greatly. During the famine of the fifties, we had made life and death our humble servants. Then, when Jinnah Sahib’s open conflict began, we came to embrace the god of death himself. As a people, the only reason we have survived is that we can live with death as our constant companion, with ease and comfort. We have dwelt alongside tigers and snakes since time immemorial—who is there to harm us?

The first blaze of open conflict has subsided, but beneath the surface, embers still smolder, flaring up here and there, only to vanish again beneath the ashes. Yet, in the everyday life of Calcutta, there is no apparent difference. Trams and buses run as before, the bustle of human activity does not cease. Occasionally, in the borderlands between the two communities, a sudden uproar breaks out—shouts, gunshots, the shops slam shut in an instant, and a few bloodied corpses are left lying in the street. Suhrawardy Sahib’s police arrive and chastise the Hindus, the body count rises by two or four. Somewhere, a motor van comes and collects the corpses, which then disappear. Afterward, life in the city resumes as before.

Byomkesh and I were living in Calcutta. Though our house on Harrison Road did not lie directly on the frontlines, we remained as cautious as possible. Fortunately, a few months earlier, Byomkesh’s brother-in-law Sukumar had taken Khoka and Satyabati westward for a holiday, so when the open conflict began, Byomkesh sent a telegram forbidding their return to Calcutta. Since then, they have stayed in Patna. In the meantime, under Satyabati’s relentless barrage of letters, we made two trips to Patna; for she would not believe we were still alive unless she saw us with her own eyes from time to time.
In any case, knowing that Khoka and Satyabati were safe brought us considerable peace of mind. In times of political upheaval, one values the safety of loved ones more than one’s own life.

The day on which this story begins fell between Durga Puja and Kali Puja. Durga Puja had, as usual, been celebrated with great pomp, and there was no doubt Kali Puja would be observed in due course. That morning, Byomkesh and I were sitting with the newspaper when Batul Sardar arrived. We paid him his “salami.” Batul was the local gang leader—a short, stocky man, with a vermillion mark on his oily forehead. Since the outbreak of open conflict, Batul’s influence had grown; under the pretext of protecting the respectable residents from the hands of other goons, he collected “salami” from everyone. No one dared refuse, for fear that one day Batul himself might take their life.
Despite the extortion, a certain understanding had grown between Byomkesh and Batul.
Byomkesh Samagra

On the occasion of collecting his dues, when Bantul arrived, Byomkesh would offer him tea and cigarettes, and engage him in conversation; much news could be gleaned about the machinations of both enemy and ally. Bantul, in these moments, would steer the talk toward business. After the war, the American soldiers had sold off many firearms for a pittance before departing; Bantul had managed to acquire some of these weapons, and now he was trying to sell them to us. He would say, “Buy a rifle and keep it at home, sir. We can’t keep an eye on everything at all times. In troubled times, it’s good to have a weapon at hand.”

I would reply, “No, Bantul, we don’t need a rifle. Something that big can’t be hidden; one day the police will get wind of it and haul us away in chains. If you could manage a pistol or a revolver instead—”
Bantul would say, “It’s hard to get a pistol, babu. Still, I’ll try—”
Bantul came once a month.

That day, as usual, Bantul took his tip, reassured us, and departed. For a while, we sat in a kind of listless gloom, reviewing the temporary state of affairs. How much longer could this go on? How long can one sit with the sword of Damocles hanging overhead? Independence might be on its way, but will we live to enjoy it? Even if we survive the battles ahead, how long can we live on crushed gravel and tamarind seeds? Byomkesh never had much work at the best of times; now, there was none at all. Where open, wholesale murder is being conducted, what use is Byomkesh’s talent for unraveling mysteries?
I said, “Give up on Bharatir and start worshipping Lakshmi instead.”
“What do you mean?”
“I mean, go out at midnight with a knife under your arm—if you can dispatch a few black marketeers, you won’t have to worry anymore. Given the times we’re living in, Bantul should be our role model.”

Byomkesh was silent for a moment, then said, “You’re not wrong; the spirit of the age is the only true law. But you know, that sort of thing needs to be in your blood. Whether it’s murder or black marketeering, without the strength of your ancestors’ blood, it can’t be done. My father was a schoolmaster, taught mathematics at school and studied Sankhya philosophy at home. My mother was a Vaishnav girl, forever immersed in thoughts of Nandagopal. So that sort of work is not for me.”

I knew Byomkesh’s childhood history. When he was seventeen, his father contracted tuberculosis, and his mother died of the same disease. No relatives came to look in on him. After that, Byomkesh crossed the ocean of learning on nothing but water and rice, carving out a new path in life through his own efforts. Perhaps he still has relatives, but Byomkesh keeps no contact with them.
A while passed in melancholy silence. Today, a letter from Satyabati might arrive; inwardly, I was waiting for it.
Suddenly, there was a sharp rapping at the door. I got up and opened it.

It was not the postman. Instead, standing outside was a person whose attire could only be described as that of a woman. But what a woman! Five feet tall, and broad in proportion, a towering, imposing figure; skin the color of polished ebony; hips wide as a water pot, a pair of unmistakable moustaches; her age well past fifty. She looked at me and smiled; it seemed—
Adimriphu 435
The lid of the harmonium was lifted.
I wondered if she was some superhuman being sprung from the pages of the Ramayana or the Mahabharata. From the harmonium came a deep, grave voice, “Are you Byomkesh Babu?”
I shook my head swiftly in denial. I did not know what business this lady had with Byomkesh, but it was best to make it clear at once that I was not he.

Byomkesh, who had not seen the woman from inside the room, came out upon noticing my predicament. He, too, was momentarily taken aback at the sight of our visitor, but quickly composed himself and said, “I am Byomkesh.”
The lady once again lifted the lid of the harmonium and said, “Namaskar. My name is Miss Nanibala Ray. I have some business with you.”
“Please, come in.”

With the sharp clack of her shoes, Miss Nanibala Ray entered the room; Byomkesh offered her a chair. I thought to myself, with such an appearance, she could never be the mistress of a household. Husband, son, domesticity—these were not for her. The “Miss” before her name was a clear testament against marital fortune. Then what was she? The matron of a zenana gate? No, not quite. A schoolmistress? Perhaps not. A lady doctor? Possible—

At that moment, Nanibala introduced herself. I realized I had not been far wrong. She said, “I was a midwife at Patna Medical College Hospital. Now I am retired and living in Calcutta. I heard your name from someone, got your address as well. So I have come.”
Byomkesh, his face grave, said, “Tell me, what do you need?”
Miss Nanibala’s appearance was formidable, but her manner was not. She carried a black handbag, which she began to open as she said, “I am a poor woman, Byomkesh Babu. I cannot pay you much—”
Byomkesh interrupted, “We can discuss money later. First, tell me what you need.”
Nanibala closed her bag, then suddenly, in a trembling voice, burst out, “My son is in great danger. Please save him, Byomkesh Babu—”
Byomkesh gazed at her for a moment and said, “Your—son?”
Nanibala seemed a little embarrassed. She said, “My son—that is—I raised him. Anadi Babu has adopted him as his own—”
Byomkesh said, “This sounds complicated. Please, tell us everything from the beginning.”

Nanibala then began to tell her story. Her style of narration was poor—sometimes jumping back ten years, sometimes leaping forward twenty, introducing many irrelevant details. But when the knots were untangled, her tale stood thus—

Twenty-two or twenty-three years ago, Miss Nanibala Ray was a midwife at Patna Hospital. One day, a young woman was admitted; her condition was dire, pleurisy with various complications, and she was heavily pregnant. The man who had brought her disappeared as soon as she was admitted. The young woman was not Hindu, probably of some aboriginal tribe, a local Christian. Two days later, she gave birth to a son and died. The man who had vanished never returned.

In such cases, the government usually arranged for the child’s care. But this time, Nanibala took the responsibility herself. She was unmarried, childless, and in the hope that the boy would one day become as her own son, she raised him as such. The child was named Prabhat Ray.

At that time, Prabhat was three or four years old when Nanibala suddenly received an insured letter. Enclosed with the letter were two hundred-rupee notes. The letter read: I have come to know that my son is with you. Please take care of him. I am sending some money for now; if possible, I will send more. —There was no name or signature on the letter.

After that, there was no further news of Prabhat’s father. The man had probably died. Nanibala was not particularly distressed. She had always feared that the father might one day come and take the boy away. Now she was at peace.

Prabhat began to grow up. Nanibala was busy with her own duties and could not properly look after the boy; Prabhat roamed the streets, playing with the Hindustani boys of the para. He received no education.

There was a Muslim bookbinder’s shop in the neighborhood. When Prabhat was sixteen or seventeen, he began working at the bookbinder’s. True, Prabhat had never studied, but he did not become a wayward or unruly youth. He devoted himself to his work and held his foster mother in deep reverence and affection.

Thus passed three or four years. Towards the end of the Second World War, a gentleman named Anadi Halder arrived in Patna. Anadibabu was a wealthy businessman. He needed many of his business ledgers and account books bound, so he sent for the bookbinder. The bookbinder sent Prabhat to his house. It was not convenient to carry all the books and papers to the shop. Prabhat brought his tools to Anadibabu’s residence and, over several days, bound the covers of his ledgers and account books.
Anadibabu was a bachelor. It seems he took a liking to Prabhat, for one day he visited Nanibala’s house and proposed that he wished to adopt Prabhat as his foster son.

To become the foster son of such a wealthy man was a stroke of fortune; yet Nanibala was not willing to give up Prabhat so easily. Nor did Prabhat wish to leave his mother. So it was settled that Nanibala would also live with Prabhat in Anadibabu’s household, and in that womanless household, Nanibala would manage the home.

Nanibala retired from her job at the hospital. Anadi Halder, too, had almost retired from his professional life, and the three of them came to Calcutta. This was about a year and a half ago. Since then, they have been living on the second floor of a rented house in Bowbazar. In the post-war market, it was difficult to find a good house. But Anadibabu had bought an old house right next to his own and was having it demolished to build a new one. As soon as the house was ready, they would move into it.

Anadibabu had an elder brother who lived in the ancestral house in Calcutta. There was no affection between the brothers; in fact, there was no relationship at all. The brother had died about ten years ago, but he had two sons—Nimai and Nitai. When Anadibabu came to live in Calcutta, they somehow found out and began visiting him.

According to Nanibala, Nimai and Nitai were consummate scoundrels, sly as foxes, ogres who would devour a child. If their uncle adopted a foster son, their uncle’s immense wealth would slip from their grasp; so they tried to manipulate their uncle into rejecting the idea of adoption. At first, Anadibabu found some amusement in seeing through his nephews’ schemes, but gradually he became irritated. A few months ago, he told his nephews plainly not to set foot in his house again.
Adimriphu 437

Nimai and Nitai had indeed stopped coming to Kaka’s house, but they had not given up hope. Anadibabu had set Prabhat up with a bookshop—a tiny little place tucked into a corner of College Street. Prabhat had never truly learned his letters, but he loved books; that shop was his very soul. Every day he would go there, selling books with his own hands. Nitai and Nimai began frequenting his shop. They never bought anything, only stood there, eyes wide, staring at Prabhat; then, wordlessly, they would slip out of the shop.

The look in their eyes was as terrifying as a tiger’s glare. They never spoke, but Prabhat had no doubt about their intentions. Prabhat was a good-natured boy, and, frightened, he came and told Nonibala; Nonibala, in turn, told Anadibabu. Anadibabu hired a Gurkha—so long as the shop remained open, the Gurkha would stand guard, khukuri in hand. The cousins’ visits to the shop ceased. Yet, even so, the fear that haunted Prabhat and Nonibala did not abate. It was as if two pairs of invisible eyes were always watching them, tracking their every move.

Besides, another matter had brought unrest to the household. Prabhat had taken a liking to a girl; she was the daughter of a refugee family from East Bengal, skilled in music, and quite beautiful. At some gathering, Prabhat had heard her sing and had spoken of her to Nonibala. Anadibabu had been searching for a bride for Prabhat; hearing of this girl from Nonibala, he said he would go see her himself, and if he approved, he would arrange the marriage.

Anadibabu went to see the girl and declared that Prabhat could not marry her. He offered no explanation, but Nonibala was convinced that Nimai and Nitai had a hand in the matter. Be that as it may, from that point on, a new kind of turmoil seemed to fester beneath the surface. Nonibala grew fearful. In these turbulent times, what if some misfortune befell Prabhat? What if a goonda stabbed him? There was nothing Nimai and Nitai would not dare. Now, Byomkesh-babu, you must, by any means, save Prabhat’s life.
chapters.summary: Gang leader Batul Sardar extorts protection money, offering firearms for sale amidst Calcutta's simmering violence.

chapters.title: Nonibala’s Plea
paragraphs: Two

Byomkesh listened with closed eyes to Nonibala’s rambling, wordy tale; when she finished, he opened his eyes. Suppressing his irritation, he said as politely as possible, “Miss Ray, what can I do in such a matter? Even if your suspicions are correct, I cannot follow your son around like an armed guard. I think, under the circumstances, it would be best to go to the police.”
Nonibala replied, “I mentioned the police to Anadibabu, and he flew into a rage; he said—there’s no need to stir up trouble over this, and if you’re so afraid for your lives, go back to Patna.”
Byomkesh said, “Then what else do you suggest should be done?”

Nonibala’s voice grew tremulous, on the verge of tears. “What can I say, Byomkesh-babu? Please, find some way. I have no one but Prabhat—I'm a helpless woman—” and with that, she dabbed at her eyes with the end of her sari.
Though no one, seeing Nonibala’s appearance, would ever mistake her for a helpless woman, still, her...
Byomkesh Samagra

It must be admitted that the heart in question is that of a helpless woman. She loves her adopted son as dearly as if he were her own flesh and blood, and, fearing misfortune for him, she has become excessively anxious. Perhaps her fears are unfounded, but even so, they cannot be dismissed.
For a while, Byomkesh watched Nanibala’s tearful outpouring with a look of irritation. Suddenly, in a harsh voice, he asked, “Where do the two nephews stay?”
Nanibala lifted her hopeful eyes from the edge of her sari. “They live under the lemon tree. Are you—?”
“What’s the address? What number?”
“That I don’t know—Prabhat knows. Are you going to see them, Byomkesh Babu? If you scold them properly, they’ll be frightened—”

“If I go to scold them, they might end up scolding me instead. I just want to see them once. If I see them, I’ll be able to guess if they’re hiding something. Prabhat knows their address? What’s Prabhat’s address—meaning, your house address?”
“House number 172/2, Bowbazar Street. But there—it's better if you don’t go to the house. Anadibabu—”
“Anadibabu might not like it. Very well, then. Tell me the address of Prabhat’s shop.”
“Prabhat’s shop—I don’t know the address—but the name is Jiban-Prabhat. It’s near Gol Dighi, there’s a big signboard hanging over the door—”
Byomkesh stood up, and in a tired, dry voice said, “I understand. You may go now. If there’s any news, you’ll hear of it.”
Nanibala, perhaps a little hurt, took her leave. Byomkesh glanced up at the rafters and murmured, “How strange you are, O world, how endlessly strange your forms!”
That evening, Byomkesh was idly leafing through a Puja annual when, all at once, he tossed the magazine aside and said, “Let’s go out for a bit.”
Since the outbreak of the great war, we had stopped going out after dusk, unless absolutely necessary. I asked, “Where do you want to go?”
He replied, “In search of Jiban-Prabhat.”
We had two stout sticks ready; taking them in hand, the two of us set out. However discontented Byomkesh might be with Nanibala, her story had, in truth, piqued his interest.

Gol Dighi was not far from our lodgings. After a single circuit of the pavement, the enormous signboard caught our eye. The shop itself, however, was rather small in comparison, almost dwarfed beneath the sign. It was a room by the roadside, with a little cubicle behind. By the main door stood a squat, sharp-eyed Gurkha.

We entered the shop; the Gurkha cast us a sidelong glance but said nothing. I saw that the walls were crammed with books up to the rafters, making the room seem even narrower. On the shelves, ten or twelve copies of the same book were stacked side by side. Books from various publishers, but seemingly none from their own press. Even two or three of my own books were there.
But the shopkeeper was nowhere to be seen; there was no one at the counter.
Behind the counter, the door to the cubicle stood slightly ajar. Through the gap, as much as could be seen—
Adimriphu 439

I saw that inside, a small cot had been laid out, and upon it sat a young man, his head bowed, binding the cover of a book. Above his head, a bare electric bulb glowed; all around, papers, pieces of cardboard, pots of glue, and a fearsome-looking paper-cutting knife lay scattered. Amidst this chaos, the young man sat, utterly absorbed in his work.

Byomkesh cleared his throat a little loudly. The young man raised his head, wiped the glue from his fingers with a torn rag, and came to stand behind the counter; he asked no questions, only gazed at us with an inquiring look.

Now I observed him properly. In appearance, there was nothing to distinguish him from the countless ordinary young men of Bengal. His height was about five and a half feet, his skin a dusky, grimy brown; his face and frame a little lean. The line of a moustache above his lip had not yet filled out; his teeth were good to look at, but their shape was somehow wild, perhaps a trace of some ancient maternal blood. There was a hint of distraction in his gaze, but this was not an expression of mind—rather, a peculiarity in the structure of his eyes. His hair was somewhat rough and unkempt, showing no sign of care. He wore a loose, open-collared panjabi with sleeves rolled up. Altogether, the picture he presented was utterly commonplace and unremarkable.
Byomkesh said, "Are you Prabhat Kumar Ray, the proprietor of Jiban-Prabhat?"
The young man replied, "My name is Prabhat Haldar."
"Oh—yes—that’s right. You are Anadi Babu’s—" Byomkesh hesitated a little.
"Adopted son," Prabhat completed Byomkesh’s unfinished sentence in a detached tone, then asked Byomkesh, "And you are?"
"My name is Byomkesh Bakshi."
At last, Prabhat seemed a little more animated, studying Byomkesh, then turned his gaze to me.
"Then you must be Ajit Babu?"
"Yes."
Ignoring Byomkesh entirely, Prabhat came and stood before me, and with respectful eagerness said, "Namaskar. I will come to see you sometime."
"To see me?"
"Yes. I have some need. Your address—?"
I gave him my address and said, "Come if you wish. But I can’t imagine what business you might have with me."
"I’ll tell you then. —Now, what do you want? Besides new books, I have some excellent old ones too; I bind and sell old books. You won’t find those in any other shop."
Byomkesh said, "For now, we’ve come to get the address of Nimai and Nitai from you."

Prabhat turned to Byomkesh, blinking several times as if to take in this new subject; then he said, "Nimai and Nitai’s address? They live—" Prabhat gave the address, a number on Madhu Baral Lane. But he showed no curiosity as to why we wanted Nimai and Nitai’s address.
"Thank you."
"Do come. But I will come to see you one day."
"Please do."

We stepped out of the shop. There was still plenty of daylight left; the winter evening smoldered slowly, like a fire made from coconut husks—reluctant to die out. Byomkesh said, “Come, let’s go see Nimai and Nitai. They’re close by.” After we had walked a while, he remarked, “Prabhat binds his own books, can’t let go of his old trade! The boy seems rather lackluster—there’s no spark in him at all.”
I said, “I wonder why he needs me?”
Byomkesh cocked an eyebrow at me and replied, “Haven’t you figured it out yet? He wants to publish your book. Seems none of the established writers have given him their work. Now you’re his hope.”
I said, “Not ‘prothitjyasha’—it’s ‘prathitjyasha’.”
He stifled a laugh; I realized the mistake was deliberate. I continued, “Anyway, he does seem eager to publish books. Even if he’s not well-read, he appreciates literature. That’s no small thing.”
Byomkesh fell silent for a while, then, almost absentmindedly, muttered, “The owl calls to the she-owl—your screech is a treat.”
Lately, Byomkesh had taken to uttering such disconnected phrases that made no sense at all.

We arrived at Madhu Baral’s lane. This alley was no recent addition; it must have dated back to the time of Job Charnock. The houses on either side were brick-built, pressed close together, somehow managing to stand upright by leaning on each other.

I spotted the house by the number above the door. It was dilapidated, but like an old man with dyed hair and polished teeth, it tried to maintain an air of dignity. The main door was slightly ajar, revealing a narrow passageway inside, like a lane within a lane. There was no one in sight.
Byomkesh gestured for me to follow and stepped inside. The tunnel-like corridor ended at a door on the right. We stopped in front of it.

A dimly lit room. It was crammed with furniture—almirahs, tables, chairs, sofas, a takhtposh—there was barely room to move. All the furniture was old, not a single piece less than fifty years; the room looked like a warehouse of antiques. In the middle, on a faded rug spread over the takhtposh, two men were cleaning guns. Double-barreled shotguns, their butts adorned with all manner of strange, intricate carvings—these guns, too, seemed relics of a bygone era. One man was oiling the mechanism, the other cleaning the barrel with a wad of cloth.

The two men looked almost identical—the same age, the same build, the same manner. Describe one, and you’d have described them both. Around thirty, stocky and broad, with round, cherubic faces, dusky complexions, and a ring of fat around their eyes that gave them a vaguely Mongolian look. Their hair was cropped short and even. They wore lungis and fatuas. There were a few minor differences, but nothing significant. There could be no doubt—these were Nimai and Nitai.
As soon as we reached the doorway, both of them looked up at us in unison. The glare of those two pairs of fierce eyes seemed to shove us back. Then, together, they demanded, “What do you want?”
Their tone was harsh, with not a trace of courtesy. I looked helplessly at Byomkesh. Byomkesh, with easy politeness, asked, “Is this Anadi Halder’s house?”
For a moment, the brothers seemed bewildered. Exchanging questioning glances, they replied in chorus, “No.”
Adimriphu 441

Byomkesh asked again, “Does Anadi Babu not live here?” A curt reply—“No.” Byomkesh, as if embarrassed, said, “It seems I have the wrong address. Does any relative of Anadi Babu live in this house? Are you—” The two brothers exchanged glances once more. One of them said, “Why do you need to know that?” “It’s only that, if you are his relatives, you might be able to give me his address.” The answer came, “Nothing will come of it here. You can leave.” Byomkesh gazed at them for a moment with steady eyes, then said in a slightly sardonic tone, “I see you have guns. I hope you have licenses for them.” We turned to leave. The unwavering gaze of the two brothers followed us as we went. Once outside, I breathed a sigh of relief—“What uncivilized men.” As we made our way back home, Byomkesh said, “Not uncivilized—cautious. There’s a type of people here, old residents of Calcutta; once they were prominent, now their fortunes have declined; they have no means of earning, so they cling to whatever their ancestors left behind. They try to maintain the old ways with rotting houses, broken furniture, and tattered quilts. Their caution knows no bounds; they don’t mix with outsiders, lest someone slip away with a scrap of their ragged quilt. Except for a few old friends and relatives, they keep no relations with anyone; if someone tries to make acquaintance, they grow suspicious, thinking there must be some ulterior motive. So their behavior towards strangers is naturally harsh. They are at once timid and sharp-tongued, greedy and restrained. They are strange creatures.” I asked, “What did you make of those two brothers?” Byomkesh replied, “Nonibala Devi did not lie. A pair of cats; but not dry cats, wet ones.” I asked, “Do you think they could harm Prabhat?” Byomkesh said, “A house cat, if it goes to the wild, becomes a wildcat. If their interests are threatened, they too can show their true colors.” Evening was thickening, the streetlights had come on. We hurried on towards home.
chapters.summary: Nonibala pleads for help. Byomkesh visits two suspicious nephews, who deny knowing Anadi Halder.

chapters.title: A Visit to Anadi Halder
paragraphs: Three

The next morning, after finishing the newspaper, Byomkesh paced restlessly for a while, then said, “Nothing to do, so let’s roast some puffed rice. Come, let’s go pay Anadi Halder a visit. We met the nephews, but not the uncle—that wouldn’t look good.” I said, “You asked the nephews for the uncle’s address. What will you ask the uncle?” Byomkesh smiled, “Something will come to mind.” Around half past nine, we set out. I hadn’t known the numbering of Bowbazar ran from one end to the other, so we were heading towards Sealdah, checking the numbers as we went. After a while, we ran into Batul Sardar on the footpath. Byomkesh asked, “Well, Batul, does this neighborhood fall under your territory too?” Batul only grinned with his oily face, then shot back with a question of his own, “What brings you gentlemen to this part of town?”
Byomkesh Samagra

“Karta? Do you need something?” Byomkesh replied, “Yes. —Can you tell me where 172/2 is?” A sudden flicker of caution flashed in Batul’s eyes. Then, regaining his composure, he said, “172/2? That’s right next to the new house under construction.” We resumed our walk. After a short distance, I glanced back and saw Batul still standing on the footpath, staring intently at us. When he saw me turn, he quickly set off in the opposite direction. I said, “Hey Byomkesh, Batul—” He replied, “I noticed. He probably knows them.” A little further on, we found ourselves in front of the new house. Bamboo scaffolding encircled the structure, masons busy at their masonry. The roof of the first floor was already poured; the walls of the second were rising, brick by brick. A massive signboard out front bore the contractor’s name: Gurudutt Singh. Most likely a Sikh. Beyond the house, a narrow brick-paved lane. Across it stood 172/2—a two-storied house, with a slender strip of veranda beside the main door, above which ran a similar balcony, hemmed in by a railing. On the lower veranda sat a frail, silver-haired old man, drawing on a battered hookah. As we approached, he glanced at us sidelong, lips never leaving the stem. Byomkesh asked, “Is this Anadi Halder’s residence?” The old man pulled his lips from the hookah’s mouthpiece and snapped, “Who’s Anadi Halder? How should I know! This is my house—I live on the ground floor.” Byomkesh said politely, “And upstairs?” The old man, still irritable, replied, “How should I know! Go look for yourself. Anadi Halder! Always—” He clamped his lips back on the hookah. Why the old man had suddenly grown so surly, I could not fathom. We wasted no more words and stepped inside. The room was long and narrow, with a door on one side—likely the entrance to the ground floor—and on the other, a staircase rising upward. We hesitated at the foot of the stairs, uncertain whether to ascend, when suddenly heavy footsteps thudded above. Looking up, we saw a towering, broad-shouldered Sardarji rounding the bend and descending. Our suspicions about Anadi Halder’s residence were somewhat allayed—this could only be contractor Gurudutt Singh. He wore velvet corduroy trousers and a gabardine coat, his beard plaited, a tight-fitting turban on his head. He swung his arms like clubs as he came down, his eyes rolling. As he drew closer, the words muffled in his beard and mustache reached our ears. The language was not Bengali, but the meaning was clear enough—“These Bengalis won’t pay me! Let’s see how great this Anadi Halder is, I’ll wring his neck and get my money. I’m a Punjabi too, no one can mess with me—” The Sardarji swept past and was gone. Byomkesh glanced at me and smiled faintly. In a low voice, he said, “It seems Anadi Babu is not a popular man. Come, let’s see.” At the top of the stairs was a door, bolted from within. Byomkesh knocked. After a moment, the door opened a crack, and a face appeared in the gap. A face like a bhetki fish, eyes bloodshot, the lower lids sagging and loose.
Adimriphu 443

Between the slack lips, the lower row of teeth was visible. Had I encountered this face at night, in such a state, I cannot say what I would have done; but now, for a moment, I started and stood still. Byomkesh said, “Anadibabu—?”
A smile broke out on the face, exposing even more of the many teeth in the jaw. In a broken, guttural voice, the bhekti fish said, “No, I am not Anadibabu, I am Kestobabu. Are you creditors too?”
“No, we have some business with Anadibabu.”
At this moment, another quick voice sounded from behind the bhekti fish—“Kestobabu, move aside, move aside—”

Kestobabu’s head withdrew, and in his place, a young man appeared at the doorway. A thin, sickly figure, with a long, pointed chin, and tightly curled hair that seemed to spread out on either side of his head like wings. There was a certain sharpness in his face.
“What do you want?”
“We wish to see Anadibabu.”
“Is there some business? Anadibabu does not meet anyone without reason.”
“There is indeed business. The house being built next door, I believe it belongs to him. We have some questions about that house. And you are—?”
“I am Anadibabu’s secretary. Please wait a moment, I’ll inform him. This way, come inside.”
We climbed the stairs and entered the room. The young man left.

The room was bare, furnished only with a rough wooden bench. We sat on the bench and looked around. Besides the stair door, there were a few other doors in the room; through one, the front balcony was visible, the other two led further inside.

After waiting a while, I saw one of the inner doors open slightly and a woman peered out. There was no mistaking her—Nonibala Devi. She must have been cooking, and, hearing the commotion of visitors, had come to check, ladle in hand. Seeing us, her eyes widened in alarm. Byomkesh put a finger to his lips to reassure her. Nonibala slowly withdrew.
The young man emerged from another door.
“Come.”
Following the young man, we entered further inside. He pushed open the door to a room and said, “Anadibabu is here, please go in.”

At first, on entering, I could make out nothing. The room was dimly lit, with no furniture except a mattress in one corner, covered with a frayed rug. Propped against a pillow on the rug sat a man, staring at us. In the half-light, it seemed a python lay coiled, watching its prey with unblinking eyes.

As my eyes adjusted, I realized—this was indeed Anadi Halder; the resemblance to his nephews was striking. About fifty years old, short and sturdy, with a Mongoloid curve to his eyes, heavy with fat. He wore a purple dressing gown.

We remained standing by the door. Anadibabu gazed at us with dull eyes. After a while, Byomkesh spoke first, “We have come on a small matter. This is Ajit Kumar Bandyopadhyay, recently arrived from East Bengal, looking to buy a house and settle in Calcutta.”
Anadibabu spoke at last. He did not ask us to sit, and in his naturally harsh voice—

Byomkesh was asked, “Who are you?” Byomkesh’s eyes sharpened, but he replied with perfect composure, “I am his agent. I heard you are building a house next door, so I thought perhaps you might be willing to sell. That’s why—” Anadi Babu said, “I am having the house built for myself, not for sale.” Byomkesh said, “Of course. Still, you are a businessman; I thought if there was profit in it, you might consider letting it go.” “I don’t do business through brokers.” “Very well, then. Please speak to Ajit Babu, I’ll take my leave.” “No, I do not wish to discuss the house with anyone. I will not sell. You may go.” There was no point in lingering further. I found the company of this thoroughly discourteous man unbearable, but Byomkesh, his face impassive, said, “Please don’t mind, but is there any objection to telling us how much it will cost to build your house?” Anadi Babu’s rough voice grew even harsher. “There is an objection. Napa! Napa! Show them out, get them out—” The secretary’s name, it seemed, was Napa. He had been standing just outside the door. He poked his head in and said hastily, “Come, please, this way—” With a sense of having been forcibly ejected, we stepped outside. The young man escorted us to the head of the stairs and said in a slightly embarrassed undertone, “Please don’t mind, sir, the master is in a foul mood today.” Byomkesh replied with disdain, “It’s nothing. Come, Ajit.” We emerged onto the street. However much Byomkesh might feign indifference, one look at his face revealed the heat simmering within. After walking in silence for some time, he glanced at me with a weary smile and said, “There are two kinds of small men—uncouth small men and wicked small men. The wicked ones harm others; the uncouth ones harm themselves.” I asked, “Which kind is Anadi Halder?” “Both uncouth and wicked.”

That afternoon, after lunch, I was debating whether to indulge in a short siesta when there was a knock at the door. I opened it to find Nanibala Devi. Nanibala entered the room, her face anxious. Byomkesh was dozing in the easy chair, but he sat up at once. Nanibala said, “When I saw you both at that house today, the blood in my veins ran cold. If Anadi Babu finds out that I—” Byomkesh said, “Please sit. There’s no chance of Anadi Babu finding out. We went there pretending to be buyers for his new house. But let that be. Now, tell me, what sort of man is Anadi Halder? Speak plainly, there’s no need to hide anything.” For a moment, Nanibala stared at Byomkesh with her large, watery eyes. Then, like a dam bursting, a torrent of words poured from her lips—“What can I say to you, Byomkesh Babu—he’s a chamar! A chamar! No skin on his face, no control over his tongue. Not a sweet word ever passes his lips—”
Adimriphu 445

Not a word escapes his lips, not a single paisa escapes his clutches. He’s obsessed with money, but not a drop of water would slip through his fingers. And if even a pinch of flour goes missing from the kitchen, there’s no end to the trouble—he’ll grind it between his teeth. There used to be a Brahmin cook before, but after I arrived, he dismissed him; for the past year and a half, I’ve been slaving over the stove, and my body is worn to the bone. What a cursed day it was when I let Prabhat become his precious son-in-law! If I had any means, I’d stuff pebbles in that wretch’s mouth and return to Patna. Having said this much, Nanibala began to pant like a battle-weary soldier.
Byomkesh said, “That’s more or less what I’d guessed. How does he treat Prabhat?”

Nanibala paused a moment, then replied, “He doesn’t bother Prabhat much. Besides, how long is Prabhat even at home? He leaves for the shop at eight in the morning, comes back for half an hour at noon to eat, then returns home only at nine at night. He hardly ever sees the old man.”
“The old man doesn’t want to look at the shop’s accounts?”

“No, he doesn’t have the face to ask—after all, the shop is in Prabhat’s name. At first, the old man put on a great show of decency. He asked Prabhat, ‘What will you do?’ Prabhat said, ‘I’ll open a bookshop.’ Immediately, the old man gave him five thousand rupees and set up the shop.”
“Hm. And Napa? The old man’s secretary?”

Nanibala curled her lip and said, “Secretary? He’s more than that—a kind of market manager. He can rattle off English, that’s why the old man keeps him. The old man himself doesn’t know a word of English, so he has Napa handle all the business dealings, write letters. Besides that, he does the marketing, massages his hands and feet. Napa does everything.”
“Seems like a very useful fellow.”
“Very cunning, more like—he’s feathering his own nest. Just because he knows a bit of English.”
I understood—Prabhat doesn’t know English, Napa does, and that’s why Nanibala is not kindly disposed toward him.
Byomkesh asked, “And Kestobabu? Who is he?”
“No one knows who he is. He’s not a relative of the old man, not even the same caste. He’s been living here since before we arrived. A drunkard, always drinking.”
“Is that so? Has he any money of his own?”
“Not a paisa. The old man gives him shoes and clothes to wear.”
“Then where does he get his liquor?”
“The old man pays for that too.”
“Strange! And yet you say not a drop of water would slip through his fingers—”

“I don’t know, Byomkeshbabu, I can’t make sense of any of it. Sometimes I think the old man is afraid. Sometimes, when Kestobabu is drunk, he throws his weight around, but the old man never says a word.”
“Is that so.” Byomkesh seemed about to lapse into deep thought.
Nanibala then asked eagerly, “But what happened on the other side, Byomkeshbabu? Did you go to see Nimai and Nitai?”
Byomkesh replied, “I did. They’re not good people. The uncle and nephews—each pointing the finger at the other. Bitter roots, bitter fruit.”
Nanibala said in a frightened voice, “Then what will happen? What if they—do something to Prabhat?”
Byomkesh said quietly, “They don’t love Prabhat, and they could well wish him harm. But even in these lawless times, it’s not so easy to murder a man, unless—”
Byomkesh Samagra

No one commits murder unless murder is thrust upon their head. Looking at Nimai and Nitai, they seem cautious men—not the sort to risk the hangman’s noose for a killing. Consider another point. If Anadi Halder is truly determined to adopt a foster son, what would he gain by killing one of them? If one is gone, Anadi Halder can simply take another foster son, or will away his property as he pleases. In such a situation, resorting to murder would be utter foolishness. Rather—'
Nanibala’s eyes widened as she asked, ‘Rather what?’
Byomkesh replied, ‘Rather, if something were to happen to Anadi Babu himself, many problems would be solved.’
Nanibala fell silent for a moment, lost in thought. It seemed she had never considered this possibility before. Then, raising her eager face, she asked, ‘Then Prabhat has nothing to fear?’

‘You may rest assured, Nimai and Nitai are not foolish enough to do something like that. Still, caution never hurts. I have a plan in mind—I’ll put the fear of God into them so thoroughly that even if they wanted to, they wouldn’t dare try anything.’
‘What—what plan have you devised, Byomkesh Babu?’
‘There’s no need for you to know that. You should go home for today. If you hear anything important, let me know.’

Nanibala, her face overflowing with gratitude, thanked Byomkesh profusely and took her leave. Anadi Halder had a habit of taking a midday nap, and Nanibala had slipped out during that interval; if the old man awoke and discovered she had gone out, she would have a hard time explaining herself.
Afterwards, I asked Byomkesh, ‘What plan have you made? You haven’t told me anything.’
Byomkesh said, ‘Do we have any postcards at home?’
‘Yes.’

‘Good. Take a postcard and write a letter. No need to write “Shriharir Sharanam” or any salutation. Just write—“I am watching you.” That’s all. Now, send the letter to either Nimai or Nitai Halder’s address.’
chapters.summary: Byomkesh and his companion visit Anadi Halder's residence, encountering a suspicious contractor and a reluctant resident.

chapters.title: Batul’s Revolver
paragraphs: Four
A few days passed.

Nanibala did not return. The matter concerning Prabhat seemed to have withered away before it could take root. Only Batul from the sadar came by once. Batul had brought a revolver, hoping to sell it to us. Had the price been reasonable, we might have considered it, but we had no desire to buy trouble for six hundred rupees. Byomkesh offered Batul a cigarette and steered the conversation elsewhere.
‘Do you know anyone at 172/2 Bowbazar Street, Batul?’
‘Yes, sir, I do.’
‘Do you know Halidar?’
‘Yes, sir.’
‘Is he—well—one of your clients?’
Adimriphu 447

Batul smiled faintly, carefully extinguished his half-burnt cigarette and tucked it into his pocket, then spoke in a graver tone, “Anadi Halder used to pay his dues, but for the past few months he has stopped. Now, if anything good or bad happens to him, we bear no responsibility. —But how did you come to know him? Did you have any prior acquaintance?”
“No, we met only recently.”

Batul did not press his curiosity any further. Instead, he left us with an irrelevant proverb, delivered in a slow, deliberate manner as he took his leave—“It is not wise, sir, to quarrel with a crocodile while living in the water.”

The day of Kali Puja arrived. From early morning, the air was thick with the thunderous sound of drums. Whether these were the rhythms of festivity or the war-drums of a looming battle, we could not say for certain, and so we stayed indoors.

After dusk, the city gleamed with rows of lamps. In every street and alley, fireworks began to burst—tubri, atashbaji, fanush, colored torches, and the relentless crackle of Chinese firecrackers and dodoma. Crowds of people poured out to witness the city’s splendor—some on foot, others in carriages or motorcars. The sword of communal riots hung overhead, but who cared for that? Life is short; why not laugh for a day or two?

We did not step outside, but watched the festivities from our window. If anyone were to mock us as cowards for this, we would not object. But to dance in foolish joy with a garland around our necks like a sacrificial goat—that we could never accept.

Night deepened. At midnight, Kali Puja would reach its peak; the festivities were in full swing. We were not worshippers of Shakti, but of intellect—yet we had no wish to incur the displeasure of Mother Kali. That night, after partaking of mahaprasad with polao, we retired to bed.
Little did we know that before the night ended, the matter that had been lying in wait would rear its head again, like a serpent.

I awoke abruptly at half past three. The world was silent, a chill breeze drifted in through the window. I pulled the quilt up from the foot of the bed and wrapped myself, preparing to drift off once more, when a violent noise shattered my drowsiness.

Someone was banging furiously at the door. Sitting up in bed, I thought—the battlefront has reached our very doorstep; there is no escape tonight. The heavy stick stood ready in the corner of the room; I gripped it tightly and stepped out of the bedroom. If I must die, let me die fighting.
Byomkesh, too, emerged from his room, stick in hand. The front door was sturdy, but it would not hold much longer; it would give way at any moment. We stood on either side of the door, sticks raised.
The pounding stopped for a moment, and in that brief pause, we heard an urgent voice—“O Byomkesh Babu—please open the door—just once—”
We stared at each other, eyes wide. A man’s voice, oddly familiar.
Byomkesh called out, “Who are you? State your name.”
The reply came—“It’s me—Kesto Das—please open the door quickly—”
Kesto Das! For a moment, the name eluded me, then I remembered. Kesto Babu from Anadi Halder’s house!
Byomkesh asked, “What brings you here at this hour? Who is with you?”
“No one, I am alone—”
Only one man was making so much noise. My suspicion was not dispelled. Byomkesh asked again,
“What brings you here so late at night?”
“Anadi Halder has been murdered. Please, open the door. I am in great trouble.”
Stunned, I exchanged another glance with Byomkesh. Anadi Halder—!

Byomkesh hesitated no longer; he opened the door. Kestobabu staggered into the room. His appearance was disheveled, his face anxious like a startled bhetki fish. On top of that, his breath reeked sharply of liquor. He collapsed heavily into a chair and, panting, said, “Someone shot Anadi dead. I swear I know nothing about it. I wasn’t at home—”
Byomkesh raised a hand. “We’ll get to that later. First, answer my question. How did you know me? Where did you get my address?”

Kestobabu sat hunched for a while, a damp-cat look about him. At last, in a slurred voice, he said, “That day you came to our house, seeing you made me suspicious. So, when you left, I followed you. Here, at the hotel downstairs, I learned your identity.”
Byomkesh regarded him with steady eyes for a moment, then said, “Hmm. You’re a sharp fellow, I see. Why do you cling to Anadi Halder’s coattails?”
Kestobabu replied, “Anadi and I are childhood friends—fallen on hard times—that’s why—”
“So Anadi Halder fed you, clothed you, even supplied you with money for drink. That’s what I’d call a deep friendship. Well, tell me what happened tonight. Start from the beginning.”

Kestobabu stared at Byomkesh, unblinking, then said in a slightly plaintive tone, “You seem to know everything already. But I swear I didn’t kill Anadi. This evening—well, yesterday evening, I quarreled with Anadi. I told him, today is Kali Puja, you must give me fifty rupees. That started a furious argument. Anadi gave me ten rupees and said—take this and get out, and don’t ever set foot in my house again.”
“Who heard you quarrel?”

“Nanibala and Napa were at home. Shasthibabu from downstairs heard it too. He was sitting on the verandah, smoking. As I was coming down, he said loudly enough for me to hear—‘Day and night the battle of Nishumbha rages overhead—who knows when this sin will be washed away.’”
“Go on.”
“Then, around one in the morning, I came back. And saw—”
“Where were you until one in the morning?”
“No use hiding it from you—I was drinking at the liquor shop—played cards at a gambling adda and won thirty rupees—then wandered here and there a bit—”
“Hmm. What did you see when you returned home?”

“The first thing I saw was Shasthibabu downstairs, pacing in the stairwell with his hookah in hand. When he saw me, he said—‘The wheel of dharma turns in the wind.’ I didn’t understand a thing. I went up the stairs—found the stair door broken!
“Inside, I saw Prabhat and Napa sitting on the bench, Nanibala leaning against the wall, sitting on the floor. When they saw me, all three stared wide-eyed, as if they’d never before…”
Adimriphu 449

Hadn’t seen. I was astonished. I said—What’s this, why are you all sitting here? Not a word from anyone’s mouth. Then, suddenly, Napa sprang up, pointed a finger at me and cried—Kestobabu, this is your doing. You have killed the master.
“Murder! My head spun. I asked—Who? Where? Why? No one answered. At last, Prabhat said—Go look in the bathroom.
“I peered into the bathroom by the roadside. Anadi was lying there, a bloody mess. Shot in the chest. The sight nearly made me faint; I sank down onto the floor. Everything in my head began to whirl.

“I don’t know how long passed after that. The three of them spoke in hushed voices, arguing about what should be done. From their words I gathered that none of them had been home after evening; Anadi had been alone in the house. Around midnight, when they returned and knocked on the door, there was no response. After knocking for a long time, they grew afraid—perhaps something had happened. Then they broke down the door and entered, and found Anadi dead in the bathroom.

“When my head cleared a little, I said—Why are you blaming me? Why would I kill Anadi? Anadi was my benefactor, my friend— Napa leapt up and said—Don’t pretend. I’m going to inform the police. With that, he went down the stairs.

“I was terrified. The police would come and arrest me. They’d testify that I’d quarreled with Anadi. I couldn’t stay there any longer; I got up and fled. I had no idea where to go; out on the street, I thought of you.”
For a while, there was silence; Kestobabu seemed to be dozing off. But I noticed that even in his drowsiness, his half-closed eyes kept darting to Byomkesh’s face.
Suddenly, Byomkesh said, “So, you did not kill Anadi Haldar.”
Kestobabu started, his eyes wide with shock. “Eh! No, Byomkeshbabu, I did not kill him. Just think—what would I gain by murdering Anadi?”
Byomkesh said, “Anadi Haldar had thrown you out of the house.”
Kestobabu replied, “That was just something he said in anger. Anadi didn’t really have the courage to throw me out.”
“No courage! Meaning, you know some grave secret about Anadi Haldar’s life.”

Kestobabu was silent for a while, then slowly said, “I know all of Anadi’s secrets; I could have sent him to the gallows. But let’s leave that for now—if it’s necessary, I’ll tell you later, Byomkeshbabu. For now, please find a way to save me from the police.”
Byomkesh thought for a moment, then said, “If I am to save you, then we must find out who really committed the murder. We’ll have to go to the scene.”
Kestobabu grew anxious, his voice faltering, “Must I go too?”
“Of course you must. On what pretext will I go if you don’t come?”
“But—the police must have arrived by now—”
Byomkesh said sharply, “If you haven’t committed the murder, what are you afraid of?—Ajit, get ready, the three of us are going.”
Kestobabu sat there, bewildered, while we dressed and prepared ourselves. When we returned to the baithak-khana, Kestobabu rose from his chair with difficulty and said,
‘Byomkesh Babu, do you—heh heh—have any liquor at your house? A little whisky or brandy, perhaps? I feel as if the strength has left my limbs.’
Byomkesh replied with irritation, ‘I don’t keep liquor at home. Come along.’
chapters.summary: Batul reveals Anadi Halder is no longer paying his dues. Byomkesh and Ajit prepare to leave with Kestobabu.

chapters.title: Midnight at Anadi’s
paragraphs: Five
When we reached Anadi Haldar’s residence, it was half past four in the night. Calcutta, after its raucous revelry until midnight, now slumbered in the depths of the late hours.

The main door downstairs was open. There was no one in the stairwell. Sasthi Babu, it seemed, had retired to bed, exhausted. Ascending the stairs, we found the latch on the door broken; the door itself was intact, but the latch had been snapped off and flung aside. We entered the room with Byomkesh leading the way.

At our entrance, a commotion seemed to ripple through the room. Yet there were only three people present: Nonibala, Prabhat, and Napa. All three sprang up in alarm. Napa cried out, ‘Who? Who is it? What do you want?’ Then, catching sight of Kesto Babu behind us, she fell silent. Nonibala, her fleshy face agape, involuntarily exclaimed in a loud voice, ‘Ah, Byomkesh Babu.’ She did not seem particularly pleased to see us. Prabhat stared on, vacant as a simpleton.
Byomkesh cast his gaze around the room and addressed Nonibala, ‘Kesto Babu brought me here. The police haven’t arrived yet?’
Nonibala shook her head. When Byomkesh turned his eyes to Napa, she stammered in confusion, ‘You—Byomkesh Babu, that is—’
Byomkesh said, ‘Yes. This is my friend Ajit Bandyopadhyay. Perhaps you remember we came the other day. You went to call the police, didn’t you? What happened?’

Napa seemed bewildered, then startled, she replied, ‘The police—yes, I went to the thana. There was no one there, just a constable with his feet up on the table, fast asleep. When I told him, he got angry and said, “Go, go, a Hindu has died, what’s all this fuss about? Throw the body out on the street.” I was leaving when he called me back and said, “Leave the address, when the inspector comes in the morning, we’ll let him know.” So I gave Anadi Babu’s name and address and came back.’

There was nothing new in the police’s habitual indifference in some cases and excessive zeal in others; in fact, out of habit, I had hoped the police would come running as soon as they heard the news. Byomkesh stood for a moment, brows furrowed, then looked up and said, ‘You all suspect Kesto Babu of murdering Anadi Babu. On his behalf, I wish to investigate this matter. Does anyone object?’
No one replied; all averted their eyes, avoiding Byomkesh’s gaze. Then Byomkesh asked, ‘The body is on the balcony—has anyone touched it?’
Everyone shook their heads in denial.

We then entered the balcony. An electric lamp glowed against the wall, and in its unwavering light we saw Anadi Haldar’s corpse lying on its side on the floor, face turned toward the street. He wore a white thermal vest, over which was a dressing gown. Across his chest—
Adimriphu 451

The quilt had slipped off; there was a hole in the vest, and through that hole, dark blood had oozed out and dripped onto the floor. Upon the dead man’s face, a grotesque distortion had settled, like the mockery of a demonic smile.

Byomkesh bent down and pulled the quilt away from the back. I saw that on this side too, there was a neat, round hole in the vest. Here, the blood had not flowed as much—only the area around the hole was damp. The bullet had passed clean through the body.
Leaving the corpse, Byomkesh stood up and gazed absentmindedly out toward the street. In a low voice, I asked, “What do you think?”

Byomkesh replied, distracted, “This is the same man who behaved so rudely with me the other day, isn’t it strange?... The body is beginning to stiffen... Perhaps Anadi Halder was standing by the railing, watching the fireworks on the street—” Byomkesh looked toward the large house across the road. “But where did the bullet go? It isn’t in the body, it passed right through—”

If Byomkesh’s assumption was correct, the bullet should have lodged in the balcony wall. But we found no sign of a bullet or bullet mark on the balcony wall, the ceiling, or the floor. Sometimes, when a bullet exits, it takes an oblique path; or perhaps Anadi Halder was standing at an angle, and the bullet went out through a gap at the side of the balcony. But from the way the body had fallen, it seemed Anadi Halder had been facing the street, took the bullet in his chest and sat down right there, then slumped to the side.
Directly across the street stood that house. In between, a gap of seventy or eighty feet. Perhaps the shot had come from a window on the second or third floor of that house.

Finding no trace of the bullet on the balcony, Byomkesh bent down again to examine the corpse. When the quilt was pulled away, I saw that the knot of the dhoti at the waist had loosened, and around the waist was a thick black thread, like a waistband. Hanging from the thread was a key.
Byomkesh fiddled with the key, then carefully removed it and, covering the corpse again with the quilt, said, “Come, we’re done here.”
Outside, the darkness of night had not yet lifted. Along the road, lorries loaded with greens and vegetables had begun to roll by. The city of Calcutta was preparing to satisfy its enormous hunger.

Returning to the room, we found the four people who had been inside still standing just as before, none had moved. Byomkesh held up the key and said, “This was at the dead man’s waist. Whose key is it?”

I looked at each of their faces in turn. All stared fixedly at the key, except for the napha, whose face was shadowed with fear. At last, Nanibala said, “There’s an iron safe in Anadi Babu’s bedroom, that’s its key.”
“What’s in the iron safe? Money?”

They all shook their heads; no one knew. Nanibala said, “How would we know? Did Anadi Babu ever let anyone touch the safe? If you even went near it, he’d start barking—” She stopped, glancing at Prabhat’s eyes.
The napha licked his lips and said, “I don’t think there was money in the safe. Master kept his money in the bank.”
Byomkesh slipped the key into his pocket and said, “We’ll see what’s in the safe later. For now, I have a few questions for you. —How many ways are there to enter or leave the house?”
Byomkesh Samagra

Everyone pointed toward the broken door. “Only that one.” “No other doors?” “No.” Byomkesh sat down on one end of the bench and said, “Alright. That means, when Anadi Babu died, there was no one else in the house—the shot came from outside. Prabhat Babu, tell me, when did you leave the house?” Prabhat kept his eyes fixed on the ground, ran a hand through his disheveled hair for a moment, then looked up and replied, “I left with my mother—around half past eight, I think.” “Oh, you both left together?” “Yes, Mother went to see a film.” “Is that so?” Byomkesh glanced at Nanibala. Nanibala said, “I hardly ever get to see a film—once in six or nine months, if at all. Yesterday, near Sealdah, there’s that cinema—they were showing ‘Jai Ma Kali’, so I went. Dinner in this house is always over by eight, so we went to the night show. Prabhat said—” Byomkesh interrupted her, “When you left, who was in the house?” Prabhat said, “Only Anadi Babu was here. Nripen Babu had left just after eight.” Byomkesh turned toward Napa, but where was Napa? She had been standing by an inner door all this time, but now, unnoticed, she had vanished. Byomkesh looked at Nanibala in surprise, turning his palms upward in question. Nanibala silently pointed—Napa had disappeared through that very door. Byomkesh, moving with feline steps, headed in that direction; I followed him. A narrow passage, almost like a lane, then a room. The light was on. We peered in—Napa was at one corner, drawer of a table open, her hand plunged inside, searching frantically for something. Seeing us at the door, she straightened abruptly and slammed the drawer shut. We entered. Byomkesh, displeasure in his voice, asked, “Is this your room?” Napa stared blankly for a moment, then said, “Yes, my room.” “Why did you leave without saying anything? What are you doing?” Napa tried to force a wan smile. “Nothing—I just came to get a cigarette—can’t seem to find one—” It was hardly possible not to find it—the cigarette packet lay on one corner of the table. Byomkesh said, “What’s that? Looks like a cigarette packet to me.” Napa seemed to startle. “Ah—oh yes—the matches—I can’t find the matches—” Byomkesh gave her a long, searching look, then took out a matchbox from his own pocket and handed it to her. “Here.” Napa, with trembling hands, struck a match and lit her cigarette. I glanced around the room. A small space: a bed on a cot, a table with drawers, and a chair beside it. There was a window with iron bars. The window was open. Byomkesh went and stood before it; I joined him. The sky was growing pale. Through the window, the half-finished new house could be seen. In the middle—
Adimriphu 453
The alley stretched ahead like a deep chasm.
“Nripenbabu, where is your home?”
At this sudden question from Byomkesh, Nripen almost leapt up. He had been leaning against the edge of the table, taking a long drag from his cigarette. Eyes wide, he replied, “Home—?”
“Yes, your native place. Where do you live? Which district?”
Nripen, caught off guard, stammered, “Native place? Khajurhat, on the Diamond Harbour line, in the district of Twenty-Four Parganas.”
Byomkesh turned from the window and fixed his gaze on Nripen. “Khajurhat! Do you know Ramesh Mallik of Khajurhat?”
Nripen, as if his voice was choked by smoke, dropped the burnt-out cigarette and said, “Yes. He lives in our para.”
“Who do you have in Khajurhat?”
“My uncle.”
“Your father is no longer alive?”
“No.”
“Very well, what is your full name?”
“Nripen Dutta.”
Byomkesh stepped closer to Nripen, his tone taking on a note of intimacy. “Nripenbabu, you strike me as a capable man. How long have you been working as Anadi Babu’s secretary?”
Nripen thought for a moment. “Almost four years.”
“Four years? You lasted that long?”
Nripen remained silent.
“You must know if Anadi Babu had any enemies?”
Nripen lifted his face helplessly. “Whose name should I mention? He was at odds with everyone he knew. Quarreling was his nature.”
“He quarreled with everyone in the house as well?”
“He would abuse everyone. But we were his subordinates, we had to keep quiet. Only Kestobabu would sometimes—”
“Did Anadi Babu abuse Prabhat as well?”
“Not exactly abuse, but he would needle him whenever he got the chance. Prabhatbabu never took it to heart, though.”
“All right, let that be. Tell me, when did you leave the house last night?”
“I left just after eight.”
“When did you return?”
“Around one, I think. When I came back, I saw Nonibala Devi and Prabhatbabu pushing at the door.”
“Where were you from eight to one?”
“I went to see a movie.”
“You too went to see ‘Jai Ma Kali’?”
“No, I went to see an English film.”
“Oh! How did you return so late at night?”
“I walked.”

I noticed that, as Byomkesh continued his questioning, Nripen had grown considerably calmer; the earlier signs of fear and agitation had vanished. Byomkesh said, “Come, let’s go to the other room now.”
chapters.summary: Byomkesh arrives at Anadi's residence to find the door broken and Anadi's body on the balcony, a bullet hole in his vest.

chapters.title: Tensions in the Sitting Room
paragraphs: Six

The three of us returned to the adjoining room and found Kestobabu and Prabhat seated at opposite ends of the bench. Kestobabu was yawning and casting sidelong glances at Prabhat, who sat with his chin resting on his palm, lost in thought. Nanibala had sprawled on the floor, her legs stretched out, dozing against the wall. At our entrance, everyone straightened up. Prabhat rose from the bench and murmured, almost inaudibly, “Please, sit.”

Byomkesh replied, “No, I won’t sit. Dawn is breaking; it’s time for us to return home. The police may arrive at any moment. If they see us here, it might sour their mood. Let me give you all a word of advice—remember it well. Do not try to shift the blame onto anyone else; it will only harm you. The police might just round everyone up and throw you all into lockup.”
Everyone fell silent.
“Prabhatbabu, now it’s your turn to speak. Yesterday, you accompanied your mother to the cinema, but you didn’t watch the film yourself?”
Prabhat replied, “No. I bought the tickets, seated my mother inside, and then went to my shop.”
“Oh. You went to the shop after half past eight at night?”
“Yes. On Diwali night, I had decorated the shop with lights.”
“And then?”
“Then, at about quarter to twelve, I closed the shop and went back to the cinema, brought my mother home from there.”
“So, from roughly nine to quarter to twelve, you were at the shop. Was anyone else there?”
“Gurung was there, standing guard at the door.”
“Gurung—the Gurkha doorman. Did any customers come by?”
“No.”
“What did you do all that time in the shop?”
“Nothing. I sat in the back room and bound some books.”
“All right, let’s leave that for now. —Did you get along with Anadibabu?”
Prabhat lifted his eyes, brimming with resentment. “No. He took me in as a foster son, treated me well at first. Then—gradually—”
“Gradually, his attitude changed?” Byomkesh said. “Tell me, why did he take you in as a foster son?”
“I don’t know.”
“At first he treated you well, then his mood changed; was there any particular reason for that?”
“Perhaps there was. But to my knowledge, I did nothing wrong.”
Prabhat, exhausted, sat down again on the bench. Byomkesh regarded him with a gentle gaze and said, “You should go and lie down for a while. Once the police arrive, there will be no more rest.”
Adimriphu 455
‘Whether you’ll get it or not, I doubt.’
But Prabhat merely shook his head. Byomkesh then turned to Nanibala and said,
‘You didn’t have a cordial relationship with Anadi Babu either, did you?’
Nanibala’s mouth and cow-like eyes widened at once, and she almost broke into tears,

‘I’ve told you everything, Byomkesh Babu. I was a thorn in the old man’s side. He loved Prabhat, but he couldn’t stand the sight of me. Day and night he’d look for excuses; the moment he found something, he’d start gnashing his teeth. Such a vile heart—’ Nanibala stopped abruptly.

Anadi Halder was indeed dead, but perhaps the sudden memory that his corpse still lay nearby made her regain her composure. Moreover, she realized—albeit a little late—that it was best not to dwell on her discord with Anadi Babu.
Kestobabu hinted at the same, letting out a hiccup-like chuckle and saying,
‘So it wasn’t just with me that Anadi quarreled?’

Prabhat turned his head and glanced at him once. Byomkesh said, ‘That line of thought leads nowhere. It appears Anadi Halder quarreled with everyone; that proves nothing. To commit murder, one must not only have the desire, but also the opportunity.’
Byomkesh turned to Nanibala. ‘How was the cinema yesterday?’
Nanibala stared at him, mouth agape.
‘Eh—the cinema—!’
‘Did you watch the film till the end?’

At last, Nanibala seemed to grasp the meaning of the question. She said, ‘Oh, but of course I did! I watched it from start to finish, only left after the film ended. I came out and stood outside, and then Prabhat came. I returned home with him. When we arrived—’
Byomkesh sighed and said, ‘I know. Now let’s go to Anadi Halder’s bedroom. We need to look at the iron almirah.’

The six of us gathered and made our way to Anadi Halder’s sleeping quarters. It was the room adjacent to the one where we had met Anadi Halder a few days ago. Nripen pressed the switch by the door and turned on the light.

The room was similar in size and shape to Nripen’s, but at the other end of the house. A barred window stood open. Apart from a bed and a steel almirah at its head, there was nothing else in the room.

Once we all entered, the room felt cramped. Byomkesh said, ‘Not everyone needs to be in here. Kestobabu, perhaps you could stay in the other room. The stairway door is broken; the police might arrive any moment.’

Kestobabu was surely as curious as the rest of us to know what was inside the almirah, but he said, ‘No matter, I’ll keep watch over the corpse. But at a time like this, a cup of hot tea would be most welcome.’ With that, he began to rub his hands together eagerly.
Byomkesh said, ‘Tea wouldn’t be amiss,’ and turned a questioning gaze towards Nanibala.
Nanibala replied reluctantly, ‘I can make tea. But there’s no milk.’
Byomkesh said, ‘Lemon juice will do instead of milk.’
Kestobabu said in a deep voice, ‘Ginger! Ginger! Have tea with ginger juice, it’ll invigorate you.’
Byomkesh said, ‘Ginger juice will do as well.’
When Nanibala and Kestobabu left, Nripen hesitated a little and said, ‘Will you need me—’
Byomkesh Samagra

“What?” Byomkesh said, “It’s you I need. Prabhatbabu, you’d better go to your own room and get some rest.” Prabhat hesitated for a moment, then, without a word, slowly left the room. Now only the two of us and Nripen remained.

There was nothing much of note in the room. The bed was made; the sheets were clean, unused since last night. On the wall, a fresh dhoti was neatly folded on a peg. In one corner stood a water jug, covered with a glass. Byomkesh glanced around, then took a key from his pocket.
The almirah was new. Its varnished wood gleamed, tall and slender, built to last. Byomkesh turned the key and swung open the double doors. Nripen and I leaned in eagerly to peer inside.

There were four shelves within. The topmost shelf held a row of books running from one end to the other, with occasional gaps like missing teeth. On the spines of some, names were inscribed in gold—Krittibasi Ramayan, Mahajan Padabali. Byomkesh took out a few more volumes; most were cheap Bat-tala editions, though well-bound. Perhaps Prabhat had them rebound.

Byomkesh asked Nripen, “Did Anadi Halder read much?” Nripen replied dryly, “Never saw him read.” “Does anyone else in the house read?” “Prabhatbabu does. I read when I get the chance. But I’ve never seen the books in the master’s almirah before.” “And yet, from the gaps in the row, it looks like a few books have been taken out. Where did they go?” Nripen glanced around the room and said, “I couldn’t say. They’re not here. Should I ask Prabhatbabu?” Byomkesh said, “Let it be for now, it’s nothing urgent. —Tell me, outside the house, where did Anadi Halder go most often?” Nripen replied, “The master rarely left home. When he did, it was either to meet the solicitor or to go to the bank. Nowhere else, really.”
Byomkesh lowered his gaze to the second shelf.

On the second shelf were many bottles and vials. The vials contained patent medicines, the bottles foreign liquor. One bottle was nearly empty, the others still sealed. Byomkesh asked, “Did Anadi Halder drink?” Nripen said, “He wasn’t a drunkard. But he drank. I’ve caught the smell from time to time.”

Examining the medicine vials, we found most were tonics—imported concoctions promising to restore lost youth. Byomkesh asked, “Did Anadi Halder have a habit of going out in the evenings?” Nripen replied, “Not much, maybe two or three times a month.” “Ah! Anadi Halder’s whole character is coming into focus. What a fascinating character!” Byomkesh turned his attention to the third shelf of the almirah.
On the third shelf were several thick notebooks and a few files. The notebooks, bound in cardboard...
Adimriphu

It was sturdily bound. Upon opening it, we found it was a ledger of business accounts. To truly understand the nature and methods of the business, one would have to study these books thoroughly; but there was no time for that. Byomkesh turned to Nupen and asked, “Do you know what business Anadi Halder was engaged in?”

Nupen replied, “I don’t know what he did before; he never spoke about himself to anyone. But at the beginning of the war, he bought up Japanese goods. The kind of machinery needed for cotton mills, that sort of thing. He bought them cheap—”
“And then sold them at black market rates. I see.” Byomkesh picked up a file, opened the cover, and began to examine it.

Inside the file were various documents: the deed for the new house, letters from the solicitor, rent receipts, and so on. As he lightly skimmed over the papers, turning the pages, Byomkesh suddenly stopped at one spot. On a ruled sheet of paper, a few lines were written, and beneath them, a signature over a stamp.

Byomkesh took the paper out of the file, held it up to his face, and began to read it with close attention. I craned my neck to see—a handnote. Anadi Halder had lent five thousand rupees to a certain Dayalhari Majumdar, as attested by his own handwriting.
Byomkesh looked up from the handnote and asked, “Who is Dayalhari Majumdar?”

Nupen stared for a moment, then said, “Dayalhari—ah, I remember now—” He stepped a little closer and, in a lowered voice, said, “Prabhatbabu wanted to marry Dayalharibabu’s daughter, but the master saw the girl and disapproved—”
“The girl must have been unattractive?”
“None of us ever saw her.”
“But then, why lend five thousand rupees?”
“I don’t know; perhaps for that very reason—”
“For what reason?”
“Perhaps, the person to whom he lent the money, the master didn’t want Prabhatbabu to marry his daughter.”
“Possible. Did Anadi Halder usually deal in moneylending?”
“No. I’ve never seen him lend money to anyone.”
“The date on the handnote is 11/9/1946, that is, about a month ago. When did Anadi Halder go to see the girl?”
“Around that time. I don’t remember the exact date.”
“Do you know anything about Dayalhari Majumdar?”
“Nothing at all. I’ve heard from others that the girl is supposed to sing very well, has already made quite a name for herself. They’re from East Bengal, only recently arrived in Calcutta.”
“Is that so! Ajit, remember Dayalhari Majumdar’s address—” He read from the handnote—“13/3, Ramtanu Lane, Shyambazar.”
I silently repeated the address to myself several times. Byomkesh began to inspect the lowest shelf of the almirah.

On the bottom shelf, there was only a single wooden hand-box, nothing else. The box was locked. Byomkesh turned the key and lifted the lid. Inside were a bundle of ten-rupee notes, some loose change, and a cheque book.

Byomkesh counted the notes. Two hundred and sixty rupees. The cheque book was quite thick, a book of a hundred cheques; more than half had already been used. Byomkesh began to examine the used cheques.
Byomkesh Samagra
Flipping through the passbooks, Byomkesh asked, “Did Anadi Halder keep money in any bank other than Bharat Bank?”
Nripen replied, “I don’t know which bank he kept his money in.”
“Strange! A new house is being built—how did he pay the contractor?”

“He paid in cash. I know, because I used to prepare the draft receipts and get the contractor’s signature. On the days payment was due, master would leave the house at nine in the morning and return at eleven. Then he’d pay the contractor.”
“So, he went to fetch money from the bank?”
“That’s what I think.”
“Hm. Do you know how much has been paid to the contractor for the house?”
Nripen did a quick calculation in his head and said, “About thirty thousand rupees have been paid. The receipts should be in the files. If you want to check—”

Byomkesh put down the checkbook and muttered half to himself, “How odd!—No, there’s no need for meticulous accounting. Come, Ajit, we’ve seen all there is to see in this room.” With that, he carefully closed the almirah.
At that moment, Nanibala entered the room carrying a large tray with four cups of tea. “Here you are. Prabhat is lying down in his room; I’ve given him his tea.”
Nripen turned off the light. Through the window, we could see that outside, the morning had cleared up nicely.
The three of us took our teacups and moved to the outer room. Nanibala followed us, carrying Kestobabu’s cup on the tray.
Kestobabu was stretched out on the bench, fast asleep. His snoring filled the room with a guttural rumble.
Peeking out onto the balcony, I saw the morning light falling across Anadi Halder’s dead face. The flies, drawn by the scent, had begun to gather.
chapters.summary: Byomkesh questions Prabhat about his alibi, while the morning light reveals the victim's body.

chapters.title: Unexpected Visitors
paragraphs: Seven
We had just finished our tea and set down our cups when the sound of several footsteps echoed on the stairs. At last, I thought, the police must be arriving.

But I was mistaken—the police were still lost in sleep. The newcomers were three in number: an unfamiliar elderly gentleman, accompanied by Nimai and Nitai. Just as vultures sense a carcass from afar, Nimai and Nitai had caught the scent of their uncle’s great departure.
The footsteps woke Kestobabu, who sat up, rubbing his eyes. Prabhat entered from the inner rooms.

For a moment, both parties exchanged silent glances. Nimai and Nitai stood on either side of the elderly gentleman, their eyes moving from one of us to the next, finally coming to rest on Byomkesh; suspicion flickered in their gaze. Perhaps they recognized him.
Byomkesh was the first to speak. “What do you want?”
Nimai and Nitai immediately leaned in and whispered into the elderly gentleman’s ears.
Adimriphu 459

The middle-aged gentleman’s unshaven face bristled with a salt-and-pepper beard and mustache; perhaps his temper, too, was not at its best, having been roused at such an untimely hour. For a moment, he regarded Byomkesh with eyes full of irritation, then asked in a distorted voice, “Who are you?”
Byomkesh replied, “You may call me a family friend. My name is Byomkesh Bakshi.”
A sudden alertness flashed in the eyes of all three men. The middle-aged gentleman drew a breath and asked, “Detective?”
Byomkesh said, “Satyanweshi.”

The gentleman made a dismissive sound in his throat, then, turning to Prabhat, said, “We have received news that Anadi Halder has passed away. These two brothers, Nimai and Nitai Halder, are his nephews and heirs. They have come to take possession of the property. You will have to vacate this house.”
Prabhat stared blankly for a while, then turned his gaze to Byomkesh. Byomkesh said, “Is that so? We have to leave the house! But you haven’t told us who you are.”
The gentleman said, “I am their lawyer, Kaminikanta Mustafi.”
Byomkesh said, “A lawyer. Then you should know that Anadi Halder’s nephews are not his legal heirs. He had adopted a son.”

Lawyer Kaminikanta made a sound through his nose, regarding Byomkesh with utter contempt, and said, “Since you claim to be a family friend, you should know that Anadi Halder did not adopt a son. One cannot adopt a son with mere words. There must be a registered deed, rituals must be performed. Anadi Halder did none of these. —You will have to leave here with only the clothes on your back, not a stick more. Everything in this house belongs to my clients.”

For a moment, Byomkesh seemed taken aback, staring at Prabhat; then he composed himself. With a crooked smile, he said, “Indeed? You think you can seize Anadi Halder’s property with threats. It’s not so easy, Lawyer-babu. If the adoption was not lawful, you’ll have to prove it in court, obtain a succession certificate—only then can you take possession. Do you understand?”
The lawyer said, “If you do not vacate the house immediately, I will call the police.”
Byomkesh replied, “No need to call the police—the police are already on their way. —By the way, how did you learn of Anadi-babu’s death so quickly? It hasn’t even been two hours—”
Suddenly, one of the brothers, Nimai or Nitai, blurted out, “Two hours. Uncle died at eleven last night—” and stopped short, as if catching himself.
Byomkesh said sweetly, “At eleven, you say? How did you know? Were you present at the time of death? With a gun in your hand?”

Nimai or Nitai turned utterly pale. The lawyer snapped at him, “You two keep quiet, let me do the talking. So, you refuse to vacate. Very well, the court will see to it.” With that, he grasped his clients by the arms and turned toward the stairs.
