Byomkesh said, “Leaving so soon? Won’t you wait a little longer? The police will surely want to hear the nephews’ statements. Where were you all at eleven o’clock last night—”
Before Byomkesh could finish, the pair of nephews hurried past the lawyer and made for the stairs.
Byomkesh Samagra
He disappeared down the stairs. Advocate Kaminikanta Mustafi cast a heated, smoldering glance at Byomkesh before following after them.
When the sound of their footsteps had faded below, Byomkesh turned to Prabhat and asked, “You never told me before that you are not, by law, Anadibabu’s adopted son. Why?”

Prabhat stood there, scratching his neck with a look of irritation. Now, Nanibala Devi stepped forward. Until now, I had not noticed how her face had shriveled and sunk, her eyes wide and desperate. She cried out, “Byomkeshbabu, is what they said true? Prabhat is not Anadibabu’s adopted son?”
Byomkesh replied, “That’s exactly what I’m trying to find out. Prabhatbabu—?”

Prabhat licked his lips and muttered, “I—I don’t know the law. When I first came to Calcutta, Anadibabu took me to a solicitor’s office. There I heard that to adopt a son, you have to register a deed, perform a homa-yajna. But none of that ever happened.”
“So you knew you were not Anadibabu’s heir?”
“Yes, I knew. But I thought—”
“You thought that before his death, Anadibabu would register the deed and make you his adopted son?”
“Yes.”

A moment of silence. Then Nanibala let out a long, trembling sigh and said, “Then—then—Prabhat will get nothing. Everything will go to that Nimai and Nitai!” Nanibala’s ample frame seemed to suddenly collapse; she sank down onto the floor.
Prabhat hurried to her side, sat down, and said in a low, deep voice, “Why are you worrying, Ma? We have the shop. That will be enough for the two of us.”
Nanibala clung to Prabhat’s neck and broke into sobs. At least, after the death of Anadi Halder, someone was finally seen to weep.
Byomkesh narrowed his eyes, watching them, then let his gaze wander around the room before suddenly asking, “Where is Nripenbabu?”

All this time, no one had paid any attention to Nripen; he had silently vanished again. Byomkesh signaled to me with his eyes. I had just started towards Nripen’s room when he returned of his own accord. “Here I am,” he said.
Byomkesh asked, “Where had you gone?”
“I—I went up to the roof for a moment.” From the look on Nripen’s face, it seemed he was relieved about something.
Byomkesh said, “The roof? The roof on the third floor?”
“No, there’s a roof on the second floor.”
“Is that so? Come, let’s have a look at this roof.”
“Is that so? Come, let’s have a look at this roof.”

At the far end of the corridor that led to Nripen’s room was a door; beyond it, the roof. A small space, checkered like a chessboard, enclosed by an iron railing. At the back, the wall of another house; to the side, across the alley, Anadi Halder’s new house.

Standing on the roof, the frame of the new house was clearly visible; in fact, if one had a habit of long leaps, it was possible to cross from this house to that one. The wall of the new house rose up to the level of the second-floor roof, bamboo scaffolding lashed all around.
Adimriphu 461
Circling around the edge of the terrace, Byomkesh asked, “Is the door to the roof left open at night?”
Nripen replied, “It’s not supposed to be. Every night, before going to bed, the master would close the door himself.”
“Was it closed last night?”
“That I don’t know.”
“When you came up a little while ago, was it open or closed?”
Nripen scratched his throat, gazing up at the sky, and finally said, “I can’t recall. My mind was elsewhere—”
“Hm.”

We returned to the room. Nanibala Devi still sat on the floor, legs outstretched in utter desolation, while Prabhat tried to comfort her in a gentle voice. Kestobabu was just finishing his belated cup of tea, setting the empty cup aside.
Byomkesh said, “Still no sign of the police. We should be going now. —Come, Ajit, before we leave, we must put the key back where it belongs, or the police might make a fuss.”
We went out to the balcony. The flies had already swarmed the body. Bending down, Byomkesh slipped the key into the waistband of the dead man’s dhoti and said, “Ajit, look here.”
I leaned in and saw, near the string at the waist, a mark—reddish, about the size of a half-rupee coin. I asked, “What kind of mark is this?”
Byomkesh ran his finger over it and said, “Looks like a bloodstain, but it isn’t. It’s jadu—betel juice.”

We covered the corpse and came away. Byomkesh said, “We’re leaving now. Answer whatever questions the police ask, but don’t volunteer anything extra. There’s no need to mention that I opened the almirah. If Nimai or Nitai come, don’t let them into the house. —Kestobabu, please come by our place later today.”
Kestobabu nodded in agreement, tilting his head. We descended the stairs. The sun had risen, and the city’s bustle had already begun.
chapters.summary: Unexpected visitors arrive, claiming to be heirs and demanding possession of the house, while Byomkesh discovers a suspicious mark on the deceased.

chapters.title: Shasthibabu’s Curiosity
paragraphs: Eight

As we reached the bottom, we saw old Shasthibabu wandering about the stairwell, broom and dustpan in hand. He shot us a sidelong, sardonic glance. The fierce expression I’d seen on our first meeting was gone; now, his crumpled face seemed almost softened by a keen curiosity.
Byomkesh paused and asked, “Your name is Shasthibabu?”
He scrutinized Byomkesh carefully, then replied, “Yes. And you—who are you—?”
Byomkesh offered no introduction, only said briefly, “Don’t ask, my friend. I was owed money by Anadi Halder, and it seems that money is lost for good. You’ve probably heard the man is dead.”
The suspicion and caution faded from Shasthibabu’s face. With great satisfaction, he said, “I’ve heard. Last night—”
Byomkesh Samagra
—I’ve been hearing since then. “How did he die?” This last question he asked, craning his neck so that his words were almost whispered into Byomkesh’s ear.
Byomkesh replied, “Haven’t you heard? Someone murdered him. I heard you were sitting out on the veranda until quite late last night—”

With a gesture of irritation, Shasthibabu said, “What could I do? The boys from the para started bursting firecrackers right in front of the house. Just look there, how many spent tubri shells are lying around. And not just tubri! The din from those Chinese firecrackers was enough to split my ears. I thought, there’s no hope of sleep, might as well watch the fireworks. So, how was he killed? Was it with a knife?”
Byomkesh sidestepped the question and said, “So, you were sitting on the veranda from evening till late at night. Did anyone come to see Anadi Halder during that time?”
“No one. Not until after midnight, when that boy and his mother arrived and started banging on the door. Then Napa came. Then Kesto Das.”
“No one else in between?”
“No one entered the house. Though—I did see one of Anadi Halder’s nephews loitering by the footpath, near the hotel.”
“Is that so? And then?”
“Didn’t see him after that. At least, he didn’t come into this house.”
“What time did you see him?”

“I didn’t really note the time. But early on, the babus were still upstairs in the hotel, sitting by the window, playing dice. Must have been around ten, maybe half past ten. So, have you found out who killed him?”
Byomkesh lowered his head and thought for a moment, then suddenly asked, “Did you have any quarrel with Anadi Halder?”
Shasthibabu started, “Eh! Quarrel? Well, it’s not as if there wasn’t any.”
“You didn’t go upstairs last night?”
“Me! Why would I go upstairs? You’re quite a character, aren’t you? What are you getting at?” Shasthibabu was beginning to bristle.
“You don’t know who killed Anadi Halder?”
“How would I know! The one who killed him knows, how would I? You’re a dangerous man, sir! I’m an old man, keep to myself, and now you want to frame me?”

Byomkesh laughed. “I don’t want to frame you. You’re doing that yourself. You’re so pleased at Anadi Halder’s death, you can’t even hide it. Come, Ajit, let’s go have another cup of tea at that hotel.”

Shasthibabu was left speechless. We stepped down onto the footpath. Across the street, above the hotel, hung a large signboard: Srikanta Panthnibas. Srikanta was probably the owner’s name. On the ground floor, the tea-thirsty crowd had already settled in the restaurant; on the second floor, a row of windows, a few open. Byomkesh stepped forward to cross the road, then suddenly stopped and said, “Wait, let’s take a look down the alley.”
“What’s there to see in the alley?”
“Come on.”

We entered the alley that ran between Anadi Halder’s house and the new building. The alley was already terribly narrow, and now, with scattered bricks and rubble from the new construction, and the bamboo scaffolding poles—
Adimriphu 463
…have only made it more impenetrable! Byomkesh, eyes fixed on the ground, advanced slowly.

The lane was a blind alley, it did not go very far. Reaching its end, Byomkesh turned back, once more walking with his gaze intent on the earth. Then, upon reaching the side of Anadi Halder’s house, he suddenly bent down and picked something up.
I asked, “What did you find?”
He opened his fist to show me—a shiny, new key. I said, “A key! But to what?”
Byomkesh glanced once at the window above, slipped the key into his pocket, and said, “I can’t swear to it, but I suspect it’s the key to Anadi Halder’s almirah.”
“But—”
“I had a hunch we’d find something in the lane. Now come, let’s have some tea.”
“But, the almirah key—”
“Is at Anadi Halder’s waist. Yes, it is. But what’s to stop there being another key?”
“But how did the key end up in the lane?”
“Through the window. —Come.” Byomkesh took my hand and pulled me along.

We entered Srikanta Panthnibas and sat down at a table. A servant brought tea and biscuits. On questioning him, we learned that the hotel’s proprietor, Srikanta Goswami, was in a room nearby. Finishing our tea and biscuits, we entered the designated room.

It was Srikanta Babu’s office; a table in the center, a few chairs. Srikanta Babu was a middle-aged man, round-faced, clean-shaven; his countenance bore the tranquil air of a Vaishnava. He was having tea with last night’s leftover fowl cutlet, and seemed a little flustered at our sudden appearance.
Byomkesh said politely, “Excuse me, are you the proprietor, Srikanta Goswami?”
Goswami Mahashay’s mouth was full of fowl cutlet; he took a sip of tea and managed to swallow, then said, “Come in. You are—?”
Byomkesh replied, “We’ve come on a small matter. Perhaps you’ve heard—a murder took place last night in the house across the street?”
“Murder!” Srikanta Babu pushed aside his plate of fowl cutlet. “Who was murdered?”
“Anadi Halder, who lived at 172/2.”
Srikanta Babu’s eyes widened in astonishment. “Anadi Halder murdered! Is that so!”
“You knew him?”
“Of course I did. He lived on the second floor of the house opposite, was building a new house. He’d often come to my hotel for chop and cutlet. —Why, I saw him just last night.”
“Really! Where did you see him?”
“He was standing on his balcony, watching the fireworks on the street. Every time I looked out the window, I saw him standing there on the balcony.”
Byomkesh said, “Please tell me everything you saw—when, from where, what exactly. I am investigating Anadi Halder’s murder. My name is Byomkesh Bakshi.”
Srikanta Babu gazed at him in astonishment and said, “You’re Byomkesh Babu! What good fortune.” He called the servant and ordered tea and fowl cutlet for us. We…
Just now, even after having tea and biscuits, there was no escape.

Then Shrikant Babu said, “I live in two rooms on the second floor of my hotel; in the remaining three rooms, a few gentlemen keep a mess. Altogether, there are eleven of us. Of these, three have gone home for the Kali Puja holidays, the remaining eight are at home. After evening yesterday, the gentlemen in rooms 1 and 3 locked their doors and went out to see the city lights. In room 2, Jamini Babu and his two companions stayed in. They are very fond of playing dice. I play too. After seven in the evening, they called me, and the four of us sat down on Jamini Babu’s cot to play dice. Jamini Babu’s cot is right by the window facing the street. While playing, whenever I glanced outside, I saw Anadi Halder standing on the balcony, watching the fireworks. We played three rounds, and the game went on till about half past ten.”
“After that, you didn’t see Anadi Halder again?”
“No, after that we had dinner and went to bed. I didn’t see Anadi Halder again.”
“When did the gentlemen who went out to see the lights return?”
“Two of them came back at midnight; the others haven’t returned yet.”
“They are still out enjoying the lights.”
Shrikant Babu pursed his lips and let out a small sigh; perhaps he was silently expressing his regret about the inherent weaknesses of humankind.

Byomkesh chewed his cutlet absentmindedly for a while, then said, “Look, Anadi Halder’s body was found right there on the balcony, a bullet wound in his chest, the shot passing through his back. From that, it can be surmised that someone fired the gun at Anadi Halder from your hotel—”
Shrikant Babu’s eyes widened again. “From my hotel! What are you saying! Who would kill him?”
Byomkesh said, “It’s only a supposition. You’re saying that from seven in the evening, apart from the four of you, there was no one else on the second floor. Are you certain of this?”
Shrikant Babu replied, “I am certain that none of the other residents were there. However—wait. There is a servant who works on the second floor, he would know. Harish! Someone, call Harish!”
A short while later, Harish appeared—a middle-aged man in a printed fatua. Shrikant Babu asked, “Where were you yesterday evening?”
Harish replied, “Sahib, I was upstairs, sitting at the foot of the stairs the whole time. When you all started playing dice—”
“How long did you stay there?”
“Sahib, when Dhiru Babu and Manik Babu returned at midnight, I spread my blanket by the stairs and lay down. I didn’t go anywhere, sahib!”
Shrikant Babu looked at Byomkesh. Byomkesh asked Harish, “From the time the gentlemen started playing dice until midnight, you sat by the stairs the whole time, didn’t go anywhere, not even once?”
Harish replied, “Just once, for five minutes, I went downstairs to fetch a dokta for Jamini Babu.”
Shrikant Babu said, “Yes, yes, Jamini Babu did send him to fetch a dokta once.”
Adimriphu 465

‘Indeed.’ ‘When was that? At what time?’ ‘Sir, it must have been around nine at night.’ ‘Hmm. From nine at night till midnight, did anyone come up to the second floor?’ ‘No one came to the second floor, babu. Around ten o’clock, the tenant from the third floor came, but he didn’t stop on the second floor—he went straight up to the third.’ Byomkesh widened his eyes and looked at Shrikantbabu. He said, ‘Oh, I forgot to mention the third-floor tenant. There’s a small room up there, you could call it an attic. A gentleman has rented it. He doesn’t stay there permanently, doesn’t eat or drink there. But every morning and evening he comes, shuts himself inside, does who knows what, then locks up and leaves again. A rather peculiar fellow.’ ‘What’s the gentleman’s name?’ ‘His name? Wait, let me see—’ Shrikantbabu opened a bound ledger—‘Nityananda Ghoshal.’ ‘Nityananda Ghoshal.’ Byomkesh glanced sidelong at me—‘If he comes twice a day, he must be a Calcutta man. How long has he been here?’ ‘Almost six months. Pays rent regularly, never any trouble.’ ‘What does he look like?’ ‘Short and stout, round-faced.’ Byomkesh again shot me a sidelong glance and smiled faintly—‘Seems familiar—’ Then to Harish, he said, ‘Nityanandababu came around ten? Did you speak to him?’ Harish replied, ‘No, sir, he doesn’t talk. Just went straight up to the third floor with his bag.’ ‘Bag?’ ‘Yes, sir. He always carries a leather bag when he comes.’ ‘Is that so! What sort of bag?’ ‘A longish bag, sir; like the kind you keep a shehnai in.’ ‘Like a clarinet case? Does the gentleman come to the third-floor room to practice his flute in solitude?’ ‘Sir, I’ve never heard him play.’ Byomkesh remained lost in deep thought for a while. Then he looked up and asked, ‘When did he leave last night?’ ‘After about an hour. He hurried down the stairs, looking very agitated.’ ‘Oh!—Well, you may go now.’ When Harish had left with the empty cups and plates, Byomkesh said to Shrikantbabu, ‘I’d like to take a look at the upper floors. Do you mind?’ ‘Not at all, why should I? Come along.’ Shrikantbabu led us upstairs. On the second floor were five large rooms side by side, with a long veranda in front. The first two rooms at the top of the stairs belonged to Shrikantbabu. The doors were locked. Byomkesh asked, ‘Do you live alone?’ Shrikantbabu replied, ‘For now, yes. I’ve sent my wife and children to her father’s house. Times being what they are.’
Byomkesh Samagra
‘You did well.’

The first room was locked; the gentlemen had not yet returned. In the second room, three gentlemen were present. One sat on the floor, polishing his shoes; the second was shaving; the third lay sprawled on the bed by the open window, reading the newspaper. Through the window, one could see Anadi Halder’s house directly across the street. I tried to peer into the balcony, but the dense cast-iron railings allowed nothing to be seen.
In the third room, Dhirubabu and Manikbabu had only just climbed onto their beds and were yawning with a snap of their fingers. Shrikanthababu said with a smile, ‘Well, are you awake now?’
Both men stretched their arms overhead and broke their stiffness.

Byomkesh did not question anyone. After inspecting the second floor, he turned towards the stairs. The same staircase led up to the third floor, and he began to ascend. Shrikanthababu and I followed behind.
On the third floor, there was only one room; the rest was an open terrace. The door to the room was locked.
Byomkesh asked Shrikanthababu, ‘Do you have the key?’
‘No. But—’ He took out a bunch of keys from his pocket and said, ‘See if any of these fit. It may not be proper to open a tenant’s room in his absence, but under the circumstances—’
Byomkesh tried a few keys from the bunch. The lock was cheap; it didn’t take much effort. With a click, it opened.
We entered the room. There was only one window, open to the street. The furnishings consisted of a bare wooden cot and an iron chair. Nothing else.

Without glancing around, Byomkesh went straight to the window and stood before it. Below, the broad street teemed with the flow of people and vehicles. Across the way, among the row of houses, was Anadi Halder’s balcony.

Gazing in that direction, Byomkesh spoke, almost to himself, ‘Last night, around eleven... boys were bursting crackers in the street... the air was filled with bangs and booms—Anadi Halder stood on his balcony, watching the fireworks... At that moment, would it have been so difficult to shoot him from this window? Even if the gunshot was heard, it would be mistaken for the sound of a firecracker.’
Shrikanthababu said, ‘That’s true. But is it so easy to smuggle a gun into the hotel, right under everyone’s nose?’
‘Your tenants come in carrying bags. A pistol or revolver could easily be brought in that way.’

‘But could a rifle or shotgun be brought in? Forgive me, I am a son of the Advaita lineage—I know nothing of guns, pistols, or such matters. Still, it seems to me, killing a man from this distance with a pistol or revolver is no easy task.’

Byomkesh only made a sound in his throat by way of reply. Then, casting his eyes around the bare room, he said, ‘Let’s go, I’ve troubled you enough—’ He broke off mid-sentence. I saw his gaze fixed on a spot on the wall.

Just opposite the window, near the ceiling, a patch of lime plaster had crumbled from the wall. Below it, on the floor, the fallen lime dust lay scattered. Byomkesh hurried over and examined the debris. ‘It looks freshly fallen. Shrikanthababu, is this room swept every day?’
Adimriphu 467

“Is it so?” Shrikant Babu replied, “No. The room is never left unlocked—” Byomkesh stepped aside, gazing upward. “Can you tell when this plaster and lime fell off the wall?” “No. All I can say is, when I rented out the room six months ago, the plaster was intact.” “Hm. Ajit, hold the cot for me, let’s have a look—” The two of us dragged the cot up against the wall; placing the iron chair atop it, Byomkesh climbed up. From there, he could reach the damaged spot on the wall. He felt around with his fingers, then came down holding a small object. It was a metallic piece, elongated like a pencil cap, with the spiral grooves of a rifle etched along its body. A rifle bullet. Turning it over in his hand, Byomkesh mused, “How did this get here? When did it arrive? Did someone fire a rifle inside the room? Or—” Byomkesh looked toward the window, “If Anadi Halder fired from the balcony, aiming through the window, then the bullet could have struck the wall right there. Or else—”
chapters.summary: Shasthibabu’s curiosity about Anadi Halder’s death leads Byomkesh to discover a crucial clue: a fallen piece of plaster and a rifle bullet.

chapters.title: Homecoming and Distraction
paragraphs: Nine

We returned home late. From half past three in the night till half past eight in the morning, I had no sense of how the hours slipped by. As soon as we got back, Byomkesh sat down with the newspaper. I tried several times to bring up the subject of Anadi, but he paid me no mind. Once, distracted, he glanced up and asked, “Does the sky really have a tangy smell?” I fell silent, annoyed. In an ill-fated moment, I had bought Khoka a book of nonsense rhymes. Byomkesh had memorized it and now recited lines at the most inopportune moments. Last night’s sleep had been cut short, so I made up for it in the afternoon. Over evening tea, Byomkesh himself broached the topic, “Kestobabu still hasn’t shown up. Seems everyone has gone to ground.” I said, “When Kestobabu had a fishbone stuck in his throat, he came running. Now that it’s out, perhaps he’s gone into hiding.” “That must be it. But if they don’t come, what can I do? The case is quite mysterious—” “Haven’t you figured out who the murderer is yet?” “No. But whoever it is, they planned it thoroughly, left nothing to chance. Kali Puja night, the sound of bombs bursting everywhere, and amidst that, a single gunshot. Such coordination doesn’t happen unless the murder was meticulously planned.” “Who could plan something like that?” “Who couldn’t? Everyone has a motive, everyone had the opportunity.” “Who do you mean by everyone?” “Let’s take them one by one. First, Nimai and Nitai. If the uncle’s foster sons inherit, the uncle’s property is lost to them—”
Byomkesh Samagra

So, before Khuro could formally adopt the boy, he had to be removed. One of the Nimai-Nitai twins took up position on the roof of the Srikanta Hotel, lying in wait with a rifle. On the night of Kali Puja, between ten and eleven, a shot rang out. Khuro was finished—job done.
“So, the nephews committed the murder. There’s no reason to suspect anyone else.”

“There’s plenty of reason. Where did the bullet fired from the Srikanta Hotel’s third-floor room come from? It’s only an assumption that the shot was fired from that room, not an unavoidable conclusion. Think about it: where Anadi Haldar stood on the balcony, there was a door right behind him. If someone crept up from behind and shot him, the bullet would pass through his body, enter the third-floor room of the Srikanta Hotel through the window, and lodge in the wall.”

“That’s possible. But there’s a flaw at the very start. There was no one else in Anadi Haldar’s house, and the door was locked from the inside. Besides, another thing—did the bullet enter Anadi Haldar’s chest and exit through his back, or did it enter from the back and exit through the chest?”

“That won’t be known until the post-mortem is done. But whichever way the bullet entered, it wasn’t found on the balcony. From that, it’s not unreasonable to infer that Anadi Haldar was shot from inside the house.”
“All right, for the sake of argument, let’s accept that someone fired from inside the house. But who was it?”

“That’s the real question. Let’s see who had a motive. At first glance, Kesto Das doesn’t seem to have any. But the man is extremely cunning and sly—perhaps he rushed to me late at night just to cover his tracks. So he can’t be ruled out. The second is Nanibala Devi.”
“Nanibala!”

“Nanibala Devi is a formidable woman. Her affection for her adopted son is in no way less than true maternal love. She didn’t know there was a legal flaw in Prabhat’s adoption. So she might have thought that if Anadi Haldar could be removed, Prabhat would inherit the property, and no one else would try to harm him. I don’t know if you remember, but when Nanibala came to see me for the second time, I said that many would benefit from Anadi Haldar’s death. Perhaps that very thought took root in Nanibala’s heart.”
“But—a woman, firing a gun?”
“Why not? What’s so difficult about firing a gun? Just as pressing a harmonium key produces a note, pressing a trigger fires a bullet. Cooking kumro-chenchki is far more complicated.”
“But Nanibala was watching ‘Jai Ma Kali’.”

“She went to see ‘Jai Ma Kali’, but what proof is there that she was in the theatre the whole time? She didn’t know anyone there; perhaps after the film started, she slipped out of the dark hall, did what she had to do, and returned to her seat.”
“Where did she get a gun?”
“Oh, you fool! When people like Bontul Sardar are running around smuggling stolen guns, is there any shortage of firearms? For five rupees, you can rent a gun.”
Adimriphu 469
“Hm. And then?”

“And then, Prabhat. Prabhat, of course, knew he was not Anadi Halder’s foster son, but he might have had other motives. He owns his own shop; even if Anadi Halder died, he would not lack for food or clothing. He might have thought that after Anadi Halder’s death, his nephews would no longer try to harm him. Perhaps, to save his own life from the nephews, he killed Anadi Halder.”
“You consider that a strong motive?”
“It may not be a very strong motive, but a mountain can grow from a molehill. Prabhat wanted to marry a girl, and Anadi Halder broke off the match. That’s no small motive either.”

I smiled. Byomkesh said, “Don’t laugh. What seems trivial to you may be a mountain to someone else. You’ve never been in love, you don’t know what love is. For love, a man can kill, can go to the gallows, can lose everything—”
“All right, all right, I admit, Prabhat could be the murderer too.”
“But there’s one thing. Prabhat was in his shop the whole time, and there was a Gurkha guard at the door. If his alibi is solid—”
“It’s likely to be solid. Prabhat wouldn’t tell a lie that could be so easily exposed. Go on.”

“Then there’s Napa.” Byomkesh took out the key he’d found in the pocket, turning it over and over in his hand. “Two things we need to know for certain: is this Anadi Halder’s key, and who threw it into the alley?”
I said, “So your suspicion falls on Napa, doesn’t it? Let’s suppose this is Anadi Halder’s almirah key and Napa threw it into the alley. What does that prove?”
“It may prove nothing, but it does cast suspicion on Napa. There might have been a lot of cash in the almirah—”
This was a new possibility. I asked, “So where do we stand? Who’s the culprit? Nimai-Nitai? Kestobabu? Nanibala? Prabhat? Napa? Or someone else?”
“There could be one more.”
“Who else?”
“Batul Sadri.”
“Batul! Why would he want to kill Anadi Halder?”

“Extorting protection money is Batul’s profession. Anadi Halder had stopped paying. If, seeing him, the others stopped paying too? That’s why Anadi Halder needed to be punished—let everyone see the consequences and fall in line.”
Putiram came in and took away the tea cups. Byomkesh, lighting a cigarette, said, “A Dom is blind in the bamboo grove. Whom to keep, whom to cast aside—like Sriradhi and Chandravali.”
We both smoked in silence. When the clock struck a quarter past four, there was a knock at the door.

I opened it to find Kestobabu. At last, Kestobabu had arrived. But this was not the frightened, drunken Kestobabu of the morning—this was a brisk, smart Kestobabu. He wore freshly pressed clothes, and a self-assured, gentle smile played on his toothy face. The man seemed completely transformed.
He took the chair opposite Byomkesh. Byomkesh, still absorbed in examining the key in his hand, looked up and asked, “Any news? Did the police come?”
Byomkesh Samagra
Kestobabu examined the key, but not a flicker of reaction crossed his face.
In response to the question, he clicked his tongue and said, “He came at eleven o’clock. What a kingdom of Ram we live in.”
Byomkesh pocketed the key and asked, “And then what happened?”
“What else? The daroga threatened everyone, opened Anadi’s almirah, found a bundle of notes and stuffed them into his pocket, then took the corpse away and left.”
Byomkesh sat silent for a while, then asked, “Didn’t he question any of you?”
“He only asked where we were last night, nothing else. Didn’t even bother to write a single line. Came in with a bang, left with a bang.”

Byomkesh sighed and said, “Well, Anadi Halder has found his peace. Who killed him will never be known, and I doubt we’ll even get a post-mortem report. Perhaps it’s for the best—you all won’t have to suffer.”
Kestobabu said, “Those who were meant to benefit have benefited—what good has it done me, Byomkeshbabu? I won’t be able to stay there much longer.”
“Why?”

“Nonibala is after me, wants to throw me out. Now that Anadi is gone, the woman’s boldness has grown. Just see—when I was leaving, I asked her for a cup of tea. She snapped at me, said, ‘No tea now, go have tea at the shop.’”
After a moment’s silence, Byomkesh asked, “So what do you plan to do now?”
“I’ll have to make some arrangement. At this age, work won’t suit me anymore.” With that, Kestobabu bared two rows of teeth in a grin.
Byomkesh said, “You’re not so old—still fit to work.”
“I’ve lost the habit, Byomkeshbabu. Ha ha—well, I’ll take your leave for today.”
He rose to go.
“Sit, sit, have some tea before you leave.”
Kestobabu sat back down. Byomkesh called out to Putiram to bring tea and some snacks.

Kestobabu said cheerfully, “You’re a gentleman, you understand compassion. Does everyone? The world is selfish—unless you squeeze their throats, no one gives you anything. Anadi has left me completely high and dry—” He glanced sidelong at Byomkesh. “Tea is a fine thing, but you know, I’ve picked up a bad habit—by evening, tea alone doesn’t intoxicate me anymore.” He laughed, a dry, throaty laugh.
Byomkesh ignored the hint. “Did anyone else come besides the police? Nimai, Nitai?”
Kestobabu replied, “Nimai and Nitai didn’t come. But Gurudutt Singh showed up and made quite a racket.”
“Gurudutt Singh, the contractor—”

“Yes. He arrived just after the police left. Started shouting, ‘I did fifty thousand rupees’ worth of work, got only thirty thousand, today Anadi Halder was to give me ten thousand, now he’s dead—who’ll pay me now?’ I said, ‘Sir, how should we know who’ll pay you? Go to Anadi’s heirs, go to the thana, go to the court, but leave here.’”
Adimriphu 471
...to go. Does he want to leave? With great difficulty, I managed to bid him farewell.'

Byomkesh, lost in thought, said, 'Anadi Halder told the contractor he would give him ten thousand rupees today... Yesterday was a bank holiday, which means he must have withdrawn the money from the bank the day before yesterday, that is—'
Kestobabu interjected, 'From the bank?'
'Yes, where else would he get that much money if not from the bank?'
Kestobabu changed his tone and said, 'Of course, of course. I know nothing of these matters! Just a humble trader, ha ha—'
Byomkesh said, 'Let that be. You are a man of the house, you know the pulse of the family—can you not guess who committed the murder?'
Kestobabu kept his head bowed for a while, then looked up. 'Let me tell you the truth—no one from the family did this.'
'You have no suspicions about anyone?'

'Suspicions? I suspect everyone, but I cannot believe it. This is the work of those two nephews. Think about it—what would the family gain by killing Anadi? All of them lived off Anadi’s bounty. Now things have come to such a pass that in a couple of days, there won’t even be food on the stove.'
'Why wouldn’t there be food? Nripen was a salaried servant—he’ll find work elsewhere. And Prabhat? He has his shop.'
'Will the shop remain? The nephews will file a suit and seize it.'
'Even if they do, they won’t starve. Prabhat, if nothing else, can work as a stationer and feed himself.'
'Stationer’s work!' Kestobabu shot a sharp glance at Byomkesh and stared at him.
'You didn’t know? Prabhat knows the stationer’s trade—he learned it as a boy, working in a stationer’s shop.'

Putiram arrived with tea and refreshments. Kestobabu picked up a plate and busied himself with the food, but his eyes remained deeply thoughtful. Only once did he mutter under his breath, 'How strange! I had no idea.'
Byomkesh said, 'What’s so strange about not knowing? Stationer’s work isn’t such a noble profession that one would go about beating the drums about it.'
Kestobabu looked up with sly eyes and said, 'That’s true.'
When the meal was over, Byomkesh offered him a cigarette and said, 'This morning, you said you knew all of Anadi Halder’s secrets, that if you wished, you could have him swinging from the gallows—'

Kestobabu sprang to his feet. 'Secrets! No, no, how would I know Anadi’s secrets? What does it matter what I said under the influence of drink? Well, I’ll be going now, thank you very much.' He moved toward the door.

Byomkesh laughed. 'Listen, Kestobabu—' He stopped at the door and turned. 'If you don’t wish to speak of secrets, don’t. I’m not overly interested. But there’s no harm in having dinner here tonight, is there? You might find it difficult to get a meal at your place tonight—'
Kestobabu eagerly took two steps forward. 'Dinner—!'
'Yes. For your sake, we might even arrange for a little liquid refreshment.'
'Are you serious? So you indulge as well! Provided Modda Didimoni doesn’t find out—'
“How is it? Yes, yes. Tell me, what time should I come?”
“Come after evening. I may have to step out for a while. But don’t worry, if I’m late returning, the servant will seat you.”
“Very well, I’ll come after evening.” With a tusked, grotesque grin, he took his leave.

Byomkesh flicked his eyes at me and said, “Kesto Das won’t say a word to us in broad daylight. —Ajit, you go to the liquor shop and buy a bottle of five-star. Nasik whisky will do. Meanwhile, I’ll instruct Putiram.”
chapters.summary: Byomkesh questions the nephews' guilt, suggesting the murder was an inside job. He considers Kesto Das and Nanibala Devi as suspects.

chapters.title: An Evening’s Trap
paragraphs: Ten
At five o’clock, the two of us set out.

Putiram had been briefed. On the table in the sitting room, a bottle, corkscrew, and glass had been arranged. At a knock on the outer door, Putiram would appear and open it, and with a face like a startled bhetki fish, he’d say, “Come in, babu, the masters have stepped out, they’ll be back soon.” He’d seat the bhetki-faced guest at the table, bring him a plate of fried eggs, and then vanish himself. After that—
Stepping onto the footpath, I asked, “Where are we headed?”
Byomkesh smiled and said, “No fixed destination. Kesto Das will come, polish off the bottle, and then we’ll return.”
“I see. But what shall we do until then?”
“Until then, let’s take the air at Gol Dighi.”
We went to Gol Dighi and began to circle it. Not much conversation passed between us; at one point, Byomkesh remarked, “Kesto Das didn’t drop the key in the alley.”

After a while, I noticed a crowd entering the University Institute—there must be some event. We’d grown weary from our aimless wandering, so I said to Byomkesh, “Come on, let’s see what’s happening there.”
Byomkesh agreed, “Let’s go. Probably a memorial gathering for some famous person.”

As we entered the University Institute, we ran into Indubabu. He was from the cinema world, and a musician as well—he’d come to attend the event. Byomkesh’s guess was correct: the film fraternity was mourning the death of one of their stalwarts with music and dance. I introduced Byomkesh to Indubabu. He took us to a row near the front and seated us, then sat down beside us himself.
On stage, I recognized a few familiar faces from the theatre, and some I didn’t know. The chairman was an elderly, silver-haired actor.

Among those on stage, one woman’s face drew my particular attention. Unfamiliar, not beautiful, but striking. Not slender, but full-figured; her complexion could be called fair, and a mass of hair tumbled in curls at her neck. What is called sexual allure—this young woman possessed it in abundance. A burly young man sat pressed close beside her, occasionally leaning in to whisper in her ear.
Adimriphu 473
The song that was playing came to an end. The president, holding a slip of paper, stood up and announced, “Now Kumari Shiuli Majumdar will sing—Kotha Jao Phire Chao Durer Pathik.”

The young woman I had been observing was indeed named Shiuli Majumdar. With a composed, measured step, she came forward and took her seat. The burly young man sat beside her with his tabla. The song began. Her voice was sweet, rounded, bewitchingly melodious. I closed my eyes and listened. Then, jolted by Byomkesh’s elbow, my reverie was broken. Byomkesh whispered in my ear, “Hey, look to your left.”

I turned my gaze cautiously to the left. Except for a few empty chairs, Prabhat was sitting in the front row. His face bore an absorbed, meditative expression, his unwavering gaze fixed on the singer. Prabhat, it seemed, had not noticed us; had he done so, he could not have appeared so engrossed. I turned to glance at Byomkesh—he was listening to the song with a faint, crooked smile on his lips.
A flash of lightning seemed to streak through my mind. Shiuli Majumdar—the very woman Prabhat had wished to marry—was this her?...
Shiuli Majumdar’s song ended. After that, a few others performed. I noticed that once Shiuli’s song was over, Prabhat quietly slipped out.
Before the gathering concluded, we too rose to leave. Indubabu accompanied us to the door. Byomkesh asked him, “That girl named Shiuli Majumdar—she sings beautifully! Is she from the movies?”
Indubabu replied, “No, not yet. But now that she’s got Gadananda, it won’t be long.”
“Gadananda?”
“The man who was playing the tabla. He’s a film agent. His profession is to teach music to girls from respectable families, but if he finds a suitable one, he drags her into the movies.”
“Is that so! Is his real name Gadananda?”
“His name is Jagadananda. In the film world, everyone calls him Gadananda. He’s ruined many a girl.”
“Do you know Shiuli’s father’s name?”
“I think I heard it—yes, Dayalhari Majumdar. Recently arrived from East Bengal.”
We returned home at seven o’clock.

The door was ajar; entering, we found Kestobabu kneeling on the takhtposh, his right index finger transformed into a gun, aiming steadily at the corner of the room. The liquor bottle lay on its side, empty. Kestobabu did not notice our arrival; he fired at the upper corner of the room—“Gudum—Phiss.”
Of course, he made the sound with his mouth.
Byomkesh asked, “Kestobabu, what’s going on?”
Kestobabu replied, “Shh, the bird will fly away. —Gudum—Phiss.”
Byomkesh burst out laughing, “Oh, you’re hunting birds. So, how many have you bagged?”
Kestobabu lowered his gun-hand and replied matter-of-factly, “I’ve shot three hotel doves.” A faint smile of satisfaction played on his slack face.
Byomkesh said, “Very good, very good. But why ‘Gudum—Phiss’? I understand ‘Gudum’ for the gunshot, but what’s ‘Phiss’?”
Kestobabu replied, “Don’t you get it? ‘Gudum’ is the sound of the gun, and ‘Phiss’ is the bird’s soul leaving its body.”
Byomkesh Samagra

Kestobabu lay down to rest. I saw that he had soon fallen asleep. After about an hour and a half, I woke him, and after he finished his meal, we returned to the takhtposh and sat down again. Kestobabu seemed much calmer now, the excitement for bird hunting had left him. Byomkesh offered Kestobabu a cigarette, lighting it for him. As he exhaled smoke, he said, “Kestobabu, looking at you, I’d say you must have been quite a strapping young man in your day.” Kestobabu shook his head with a rueful smile. “What a body I had, Byomkeshbabu, you wouldn’t believe it if you hadn’t seen. Broad chest, arms like clubs; I could finish off an entire goat by myself. People used to call me—Bheem Kesto.” “You must have been quite the brawler? Beat up a lot of sahibs, did you?” “Sahibs, you say? I even beat up shipyard goras. Those fellows would come ashore to drink, wandering the alleys and lanes. I’d lie in wait—if I caught one alone, a couple of blows and he’d be out cold. Ha ha.” “You’re just the sort of man I like. Tell me, have you ever killed a man?” Byomkesh leaned in close, his tone confidential. “Killed a man—!” Kestobabu looked at him, a hint of suspicion in his eyes. “Oh come on, man, what’s there to be afraid of? What harm in telling an old friend? Why, I’ve killed three men myself. Ajit knows, ask him.” Kestobabu seemed reassured. “Didn’t kill anyone with my own hands, but I was in the gang. That Anadi fellow—” “You’ve known Anadi Haldar a long time, then?” “Since school. Anadi was a sly devil, but he wasn’t strong, so he always tried to rope me in. I was a good boy in school, you know, but fell in with Anadi and went astray.” “And then?” “There was a deputy’s son who used to come to school on a bicycle. One day, Anadi and I stole the bicycle, sold it in the black market. But since it was the deputy’s son’s bike, the police got involved. We got caught. The headmaster rusticated us both.” “There you go. Headmasters are a rotten lot. —What happened after that?” “What else? Name struck off, I was a sepoy! Couple of years later, the Great War broke out. And then, who could stop us? Straight to Mesopotamia. Basra... Kut-el-Amara—those were wild, heady years!” “Is that when you learned to shoot a rifle?” “Yes. My aim was flawless. When we were trapped at Kut-el-Amara and our rations ran low, we had to eat horse meat. I used to shoot flying birds with my rifle. The captain called me—William Tell! Those were the days.” He sighed. “After the war, I came back home. Became a nobody again... Then, after a while, Anadi pulled off a stunt. Got into a fight with his father, beat him up and ran away from home. Beat him so badly the old man died the next day. The family hushed it up, of course, but Anadi disappeared—gone for five years. “Five years later, one night, Anadi turned up at my place, sneaking in quietly. Said—‘Want to go into business with me? It’s a very profitable business.’ I asked—‘What kind of business? Where do we have to go?’ He said—to a small town in Bihar.”
Adimriphu 475
Business with a Marwari. One cannot run that business alone, that’s why I came to take you. Fortune will turn overnight. Will you come? Let’s go.—At that time, my luck was running low, so I agreed.

‘A nondescript place in Bihar, called Lalnia. A railway line runs in front. Behind it, hills and jungle. We got off at the station but didn’t go into town; during the day, we hid in the jungle. There, Anadi revealed the real plan—on the edge of town, beside the jungle, there’s a Marwari’s godown. The old Marwari stays there alone at night. The old man has a lot of money. We have to rob the godown.

‘At midnight, we went to the Marwari’s godown. I had an iron rod in my hand; Anadi had an electric torch and a bhojali tucked at his waist. The Marwari dealt in stolen goods; thieves would come to him at night. As soon as Anadi knocked, he opened the door. I struck him on the head with the rod. The old man collapsed, unconscious.

‘We looted the godown. Didn’t find much—about three thousand rupees in cash and some gold ornaments. As we were leaving, the Marwari lay across the threshold. Suddenly, he grabbed Anadi’s leg. No matter how much Anadi struggled, he couldn’t free himself—the Marwari had locked on with a death grip. Then Anadi drew the bhojali from his waist and struck the old man’s neck. With a gurgle, the old man died.

‘We left the blood-stained bhojali there and fled. In the last hours of the night, we reached the station and caught a train. The loot was with Anadi; he said—You get on one carriage, I’ll get on another. If both of us board the same compartment, someone might get suspicious. Go on, go on, we’ll meet again at the next station. I boarded one compartment, Anadi boarded the next.
‘That was it. From that moment, Anadi vanished. In twenty years, I never saw even a hair of him again—traitor! Betrayer!’

Grieving for his lost money, Kestobabu began to fume. Byomkesh handed him another cigarette and said, ‘Anadi Halder was a traitor, that’s why he’s in such a wretched state today. But you said you could have sent Anadi to the gallows if you wished—what did you mean by that? If you tried to implicate him, you would have been caught yourself.’

Kestobabu said, ‘There was a huge uproar over the Marwari’s murder, it was all over the papers. The police found Anadi’s fingerprints on the bhojali, but they didn’t know him—how would they catch him? Only I knew. If I had sent the police an anonymous letter—“The killer in Lalnia is Anadi Halder, he lives at such-and-such address, match the fingerprints”—what would have happened then?’
Byomkesh said, ‘I see. And when did you next encounter Anadi Halder?’

Kestobabu bared his teeth in a grin—‘About two years ago, here in Calcutta. I was walking along the footpath when I saw Anadi entering a house in Bowbazar. Where else would he go? I made some inquiries and found out Anadi had made money, was living well. For a moment, I thought of sending an anonymous letter to the police. But my luck was bad at the time—one day, I went to see him. Anadi recoiled as if he’d seen a ghost. I said—From now on, you’ll have to keep me in comfort too, or the police will find out who killed the Marwari in Lalnia. A murder case never expires…’
Night had fallen. Kestobabu spent the night with us on the takhtposh.
Byomkesh Samagra
chapters.summary: Byomkesh and his companion attend a memorial event, encountering a striking woman and a man who reveals a past blackmail scheme.

chapters.title: The Hunter Slips Away
paragraphs: Eleven
The next morning, I woke up late. Hurrying to the sitting room, I found Byomkesh writing a letter; Kestobabu was nowhere to be seen. I asked, “Where’s the hunter?”
Byomkesh looked up with a smile and said, “He slipped away before dawn.”
No doubt, recalling in the morning all that he had revealed under the influence of drink last night, Kesto Das had decided to make himself scarce.
I settled myself on the divan. “Who are you writing to so early in the morning?”
Byomkesh handed me the letter and began composing another. I read:

Brother Romesh, Do you remember me after all these years? We studied together at Berhampore! The professors used to call me ‘bomb-case’. Does that ring a bell? I heard from someone named Nripen Dutta that you’re still living in your village. You know Nripen—he’s from your para. I want to know something about him. Surely you come to Calcutta from time to time. Why don’t you visit me at my place? I’m giving you the address. When will you come? Take my love.
Yours, Your old friend Byomkesh Bakshi
The second letter was addressed to Nimai and Nitai—
Nimaibabu, Nitaibabu, I have come to know about the third-floor room at Srikanta Panth Nibas. Come and see me at once, or else the police may get wind of this.
Byomkesh Bakshi

Byomkesh slipped both letters into envelopes, wrote the addresses, and called for Putiram. Putiram was about to leave for the market; Byomkesh handed him the two letters to post, then turned to me and said, “Come, we have to go out this morning.”
“Where to?”
“Do you remember the address of Dayalhari Majumdar’s house?”
“13/3, Ramtanu Lane, Shyambazar.”

Half an hour later, we set out. It took us some time to locate Ramtanu Lane in Shyambazar. The lane was narrow both in length and breadth, connecting two major roads on either side. We advanced, checking the house numbers as we went.

We had reached about the middle of the lane when suddenly, from a house at the far end, a man emerged and strode towards us like a storm. I recognized Prabhat. He passed by us without noticing, wild hair, flushed face and eyes; he swept past us like a blast of fire.

We raised our eyebrows and exchanged glances, then proceeded towards the door from which Prabhat had emerged. There was no longer any need to look for the number. Byomkesh murmured, “He had broken off with Anadi Halder… Now that Anadi is gone, Prabhat came back… but things didn’t go his way…”
The door of 13/3 was closed. We stood for a moment, hesitating, when from inside the house…
From within, a woman’s voice began to sing—a sweet, rounded, bewitching melody, accompanied by the rhythmic beat of the tabla.
Byomkesh knocked at the door. The singing ceased. An elderly man opened the door. A pair of hard, searching eyes swept over us from head to toe.
“What do you want?” The man’s figure was as gnarled as a twisted bamboo cane, and his voice was equally dry and abrasive, tinged with the accent of East Bengal.
Byomkesh said, “Is your name Dayalhari Majumdar?”
“Yes. What do you want?” There was no invitation to enter; instead, the householder gripped both door panels and blocked our way.
Byomkesh said, “Anadi Halder is dead. Perhaps you’ve heard. I want to ask you a few things about him—”
“Who is Anadi Halder? I don’t know him.” Dayalharibabu’s parched voice turned sharp.
“You don’t know? Your handnote was found in his almirah. You borrowed five thousand rupees from him.”
“Who says I borrowed money? Lies. I don’t owe a single paisa to anyone.”
“I saw your signature on the handnote with my own eyes.”
“A forged signature.” With a loud slam, the door was shut in our faces.
We stood for a moment before the closed door, then turned and walked away. Behind us, the singing and accompaniment resumed—Bhairavi, in a single beat.

As we walked toward the tram road, Byomkesh gave a weary smile. “Dayalhari Majumdar is no ordinary man. Now that he knows Anadi Halder is dead, he’s thinking he’ll get away with the five thousand rupees. The signature on the handnote may not be his usual one—he’s probably twisted and disguised it, so if the matter goes to court, he can deny it. But that’s not the real issue; the question is, why did Anadi Halder lend him five thousand rupees?”
I said, “Perhaps Anadi Halder was in the moneylending business.”

“Even so, would he lend five thousand rupees, cash in hand, without any security? Was Anadi Halder such a fool? If you saw a monkey singing or a stone floating on water, perhaps then you’d believe it.”
“Then what could it be?”
“I don’t know. But I must find out. Do you know what I suspect?”
“What?”
Byomkesh opened his mouth to speak, then stopped. He looked up at the sky and said, “Illusions at every turn.”
After that, I asked no more questions.
That evening, we set out again. This time, our destination was Prabhat’s shop.

As we neared the shop, I saw Batul Sardar walking ahead of us among a group of men. When he reached Prabhat’s shop, Batul slowed down, as if intending to enter. But before stepping inside, he turned his head and glanced back. Our eyes met. Instantly, Batul resumed walking straight ahead.
I glanced sidelong at Byomkesh. His brows were furrowed, the bones of his jaw set hard. I murmured, “Is Batul trying to make Prabhat his next customer?”
Byomkesh Samagra
“Is it?”
Byomkesh made a sound deep in his throat.
We entered the shop.

There were no customers; only Prabhat sat at the counter, his elbow resting, his hand pressed to his forehead. His face was not clearly visible. At the sound of our footsteps, he looked up. His eyes were red as hibiscus flowers. For a moment he stared at us with unrecognizing eyes, then started and stood up abruptly. He said, “Come in.”

We went and stood before the counter. The piles upon piles of books in the bookstore always cast a spell on my mind; I turned my head to look all around. Byomkesh was immune to such distractions. He said, “We’ve come for a small matter. Tell me, do you recognize this key?”
Prabhat took the key from Byomkesh’s hand and turned it over, examining it. He said, “No. Where is this key from?”
Byomkesh replied, “That I don’t know. I found it lying in the alley beside your house.”
“I don’t know, I don’t think I’ve ever seen it. Looks like a new key. Perhaps it fell from someone’s pocket on the street.”
Prabhat returned the key. Byomkesh put it back in his pocket and said, “Any news of Kestobabu? He returned to your house this morning.”
Prabhat gave a wan smile—“Yes. Last night he went somewhere.”
Byomkesh did not say where he had gone, but asked, “So Kestobabu is still staying with you?”
“So it seems. What can I do? Can’t exactly throw him out.”
“True enough. Where is Nripenbabu? Has he left?”
“No, not yet. His salary for two months is pending… poor man… I’m thinking of keeping him on. It’s good to have someone in the shop, I think I’ll keep him.”
Byomkesh said, “Not a bad idea. Tell me, Nimai and Nitai haven’t come again, have they? Did the police seal the almirah?”
“No, the police haven’t come again. But they took the key that was on Anadi Babu’s waist. I think that was the only key to the almirah.”
“Perhaps. Now, one more question. Did you know that Anadi Halder had lent five thousand rupees to someone named Dayalhari Majumdar?”
For a moment, Prabhat stared at him in disbelief—“Five thousand rupees! Are you certain?”
“I saw the hand-note in Anadi Halder’s almirah. It bears Dayalhari Majumdar’s signature.”

Prabhat’s thin face seemed to grow even more drawn and weary; in a half-choked voice he said, “I didn’t know. Never heard of it.” As he tried to sit on the stool, he nearly missed and almost fell. Byomkesh quickly reached out and caught him.
“Prabhatbabu! You have a fever—your body is hot.”
“Fever? No, it’s nothing. Just a cold—”
“Perhaps it’s settled in your chest. Why did you come to the shop? Go home and rest. Call a doctor—”
Adimriphu 479
“Doctor!” Prabhat exclaimed in alarm—“No, no, there’s no need for all that fuss. It’ll get better on its own.”
“Listen to me, there’s a doctor I know nearby. Let’s go to him. It’s never wise to neglect an illness. Come.”
Prabhat protested a few more times, but finally relented. Locking up the shop, as we were about to step outside, Byomkesh asked, “I don’t see your Gurkha doorman. Have you let him go?”
Prabhat replied, “Yes. He hadn’t been home in a long time, so he quit and left. I don’t really need a watchman anymore—” He gave a wan smile.

In two or three minutes, we reached Dr. Talukdar’s clinic. The doctor was in; Byomkesh took him aside and spoke with him in private. Then he brought Prabhat into the room, laid him down on the table, and began his examination. We stepped aside.
After the examination, the doctor came out and said, “I found nothing in the chest or back. But the nerves have suffered a severe shock. I’m prescribing a medicine—one bottle should set him right.”
The doctor went to write the prescription, and Byomkesh accompanied him. A short while later, he returned with the medicine bottle in hand and said, “Let’s go. I’ve settled the doctor’s fee.”
Prabhat, embarrassed, said, “Oh, but why did you pay? I have money—”
“Never mind, we’ll see about that later. For now, let’s get you home.”
Prabhat’s eyes grew moist—“You’re going to such trouble for me—”
Byomkesh smiled slightly and said, “When you live in this world, you have to go to a little trouble for each other. Come.”
We took a hired carriage and set off toward Prabhat’s house. I couldn’t help but wonder if there was some hidden motive behind Byomkesh’s benevolence.

When we arrived, Nanibala Devi, hearing of Prabhat’s fever, became frantic with worry and led him to bed. She was an experienced nurse. There was no need to instruct her about medicine or diet. We took our leave.
In the outer room, Byomkesh paused. From his demeanor, it seemed he had no intention of leaving just yet. I raised an eyebrow in question; in reply, he narrowed his left eye.
Footsteps on the stairs. Nripen entered; seeing us, he stopped short.
“You?”
Byomkesh said, “Prabhat-babu was unwell, so we brought him home.”
“Prabhat-babu is ill.” Nripen stepped toward the inner rooms.
“One thing,” Byomkesh produced a key and held it out before him, “do you recognize this key?”

Nripen’s gaze, which had been open and straightforward, suddenly turned furtive. He swallowed once, steadied his voice, and said, “Key? Whose key—how should I know? Excuse me, Prabhat-babu’s fever—” Without finishing his sentence, he hurried toward Prabhat’s room.
Byomkesh stood silently for a moment, then whispered in my ear, “Ajit, wait here. I’ll be right back.” He moved lightly toward Anadi Halder’s room.
I stood alone, wondering—if someone came and started questioning me about Byomkesh, what would I say? But within a minute, Byomkesh returned and said, “Come on.”
Byomkesh Samagra
“Let’s be off now.”

Downstairs, on the verandah, Sasthibabu was puffing on his hookah, casting sharp, suspicious glances our way. The street lamps were lit. We quickened our pace toward home. As we walked, Byomkesh said, “It is indeed the key to Anadi Halder’s almirah, and there is no doubt about who threw it into the alley.”

A week slipped by. Not a sound or sign from any quarter. Byomkesh had told Nimai and Nitai to come see him at once, but they too remained silent. It was as if everything had sunk into a drowsy stupor again. Like the hush that falls after a train has left the station—this was much the same.
Then the trains began to arrive. One after another, they came. In the end, so many trains arrived that there was hardly time to catch our breath.

That morning, the post brought two letters. One was from Satyabati. She hadn’t seen us in so long, she was beginning to doubt whether we were still alive, and demanded an immediate visit. The second letter was from Ramesh Mallik of Khejurbari. He wrote—

Brother Byomkesh, so you haven’t forgotten me after all? I can’t tell you how delighted I was to receive your letter. Memories of those old, half-forgotten college days have come flooding back. Brother, I would certainly have come to see you, but for some days now I’ve been bedridden with rheumatism, unable to move. I’ve read of your exploits in books, I know you live in Calcutta. But I didn’t know your address, so I couldn’t visit. As soon as I recover, I’ll come.

I know much about the person you inquired about; if we meet, I’ll tell you everything. He’s a remarkable fellow. Once did a stint in jail. His chief and greatest talent is that, if he sees any key just once, he can make an exact duplicate. Gifted boy, but his uncle threw him out of the house. He’d made a key to his uncle’s safe and would occasionally pilfer five or ten rupees. After being thrown out, he went to Calcutta and found work, but there too he made a duplicate key to the cash box. Got caught and landed in jail. That was four or five years ago. I don’t know how you came to be involved with him, but be careful.
I’m longing to see you. That’s all for now. With love, Yours—Ramesh.

Byomkesh said, “A remarkable fellow, no doubt. There are few in the world with such a gift. Anyway, Nappa’s modus operandi is becoming clear now. Anadi Halder used to keep the almirah key at his waist—so it wasn’t easy to see! At some point, Nappa managed to get a look at it, and made a duplicate. He knew there was loot in the almirah, so he waited for the right opportunity. Then, on the night of Kali Puja—” Byomkesh broke off.
“The night of Kali Puja—what happened?”

Before Byomkesh could answer, there was a knock at the door. I opened it, and beheld a remarkable sight. Lawyer Kaminikanta Mustafi stood there, flanked on either side by his two clients. A honeyed smile played on Kaminikanta’s lips. Nimai and Nitai looked so changed, they were barely recognizable as human beings—truly, two...
Adimriphu 481

A drenched cat. Bare feet, a pair of coarse tussar shawls thrown over the shoulders, an unshaven beard, the garb of ritual impurity. The three of them entered the room. Byomkesh turned his head from the comfort of his armchair and looked once; the scorn on his face slowly curled into a mocking smile. He said, “So you have finally come, then?—Sit down.”

The three of them sat at the edge of the takhtposh. Kaminikanta said, “We’re a little late. The way you threatened in your letter, they didn’t dare come alone, they ran straight to me. And I am, after all, a lawyer; I couldn’t come without making a few inquiries first. So—”
“Where did you make your inquiries? At Shrikanta Panthnibas? Didn’t have much luck there, did you? Couldn’t break the witness? Shrikantababu wouldn’t agree to perjure himself?”
Kaminikantababu replied in a wounded tone, “Oh, come now, Byomkeshbabu, what are you saying! Breaking witnesses is not my profession; my job is to discover the truth on behalf of my client.”
“To discover the truth, there was no need to go to Shrikanta Hotel; you could have just asked your clients.”

“They’re just boys, and besides, they’re in ritual impurity. Anyway, tell me what you want to know—there’s nothing they’ll hide from you. Once you hear their account, you’ll see they’re completely innocent.”
Byomkesh observed Nitai and Nimai in turn and said, “Which of them used to frequent Shrikanta Hotel?”
Kaminikanta said, “Both of them went. But they look quite alike, so perhaps the hotel staff couldn’t tell them apart.”
Byomkesh said, “Hmm. What was the purpose of renting the upstairs room at Shrikanta Hotel?”
Kaminikanta replied, “Then let me tell you everything from the beginning—”
Byomkesh said, “Wouldn’t it be better if they spoke for themselves?”
“Heh heh, that’s true. But you see, they’re just boys, and after all that’s happened, they’re terribly nervous. They might muddle things up and you’d suspect they’re lying—”
With a sigh, Byomkesh said, “Fine, you tell it then. I can see there’ll be no difference between your words and theirs. What’s the point of wasting time?”
The two boys raised no objection; Kaminikanta recounted the story in their stead. The gist of it was this—

About two years ago, when Anadi Halder Mahashay began living in Calcutta, Nimai and Nitai, upon hearing the news, rushed to their uncle. They were fatherless; their uncle was their only guardian, and they insisted he return with them to the old house.

Anadi Halder was an exceedingly decent and good man, his affection for his nephews knew no bounds. But a group of wicked men, taking advantage of his kindness, settled onto his shoulders, began poisoning his ears, and turned his mind against his nephews. He severed all ties with Nitai and Nimai.

By right and by law, Nimai and Nitai were Anadi Babu’s heirs. They feared these wicked men would cheat their uncle out of his entire property, might even murder him. So, after consulting together, Nimai and Nitai rented a room at Shrikanta Hotel and began keeping watch on Anadi Babu’s house through the window. In their house, there was a...
Byomkesh Samagra
There was an old-fashioned telescope, with which they would try to observe the goings-on inside Anadi Babu’s house. Here, look, that very telescope.

—One of the Nimai-Nitai twins produced the telescope from beneath a shawl and showed it. It was a telescope encased in leather, shaped like a tube, which extended when pulled; Byomkesh examined it, then returned it.
Kaminikanta resumed his account:

Nimai and Nitai would take turns going to the hotel, sitting by the window with the telescope pressed to their eyes. Of course, this was nothing but childish mischief. Kaminikanta knew nothing of it; had he known, he would never have allowed such a ridiculous affair to occur. Be that as it may, after several months had passed in this manner, the night of Kali Puja arrived.

Around ten o’clock that night, Nimai went to the hotel and sat down with the telescope. Anadi Babu was standing on the balcony, watching the fireworks. At eleven, something happened. Anadi Babu suddenly turned toward the back door, as if he had heard someone behind him. Instantly, there was the sound of a gunshot, and the bullet whistled past Nimai’s ear. On the balcony, Anadi Babu collapsed. But from the darkness of the room, Nimai could not see who had fired the shot.

Nimai understood the situation. The bullet had passed through Anadi Babu’s body and, by a hair’s breadth, would have killed Nimai as well; by sheer luck, it grazed past his temple. He returned home at once, and the two brothers, after conferring, went to Kaminikanta that very night. After that, everything that transpired is well known to Byomkesh Babu.

This is the true state of affairs; there is not a shred of falsehood in it. Byomkesh Babu is a discerning man—surely he realizes that it is impossible for any gentleman’s son to have murdered the venerable Khullatata. Therefore, he must not inform the police. The police—especially the police of these times—if given such a pretext, would hound Nimai and Nitai mercilessly, tormenting the innocent. That is never desirable. As it is, the land is already smothered in injustice and oppression.
Kaminikanta finished. Byomkesh stretched, yawned, and said lazily, “They have surely applied for the succession certificate, haven’t they? What became of that?”
Kaminikanta replied, “The application has been made. But it’s a matter for the courts—it will take time.”
Byomkesh said, “I believe Prabhat will raise no objection. But the bookshop is in his name; if you try to lay hands on that, he will fight.”
“No, no, whatever Anadi Babu donated, they have no greed for it.—Then, Byomkesh Babu, may I hope you will not reveal the matter of the Srikanta Hotel?”
“I will consider the matter. If Nimai Babu and Nitai Babu are innocent, they have nothing to fear. Well then, let’s call it a night.”

The three of them rose, exchanging glances, speaking with their eyes. Then Kaminikanta, hesitating a little, said, “We have wasted much of your time today. As compensation, a small token—” He drew five one-hundred-rupee notes from his pocket and held them out.
Byomkesh’s lips curled in sardonic amusement. “My time is not so valuable. Besides, I do not accept bribes.”

Kaminikanta hastily said, “No, no, that’s not it. You are investigating Anadi Babu’s death—there are expenses involved. It is only right that they should bear those costs. Well, I won’t waste any more of your time. Namaskar.” Placing the notes on the table, he and his client departed swiftly.
Adimriphu 483
He took his leave.

Byomkesh, flipping through the notes and tucking them into his pocket, remarked, “I’ve learned how to pay a bribe today.” Then, arching his brow, he looked at me—“So, what did you think of the story?”
I replied, “It didn’t seem entirely impossible to me.”
“Could you write a story like that? Do you have the courage?”
“There are many true incidents that cannot be written as stories; if you do, they become unbelievable. Yet what is true remains true. Truth is stranger than fiction.”
The argument was just beginning to gather steam when, once again, a visitor arrived at the door.
The door was ajar; someone poked his head through the gap and said, “May I come in, sir?”—and flashed a toothy grin.
To my surprise, it was Bikash Dutta! I had met him about a year ago, in connection with the zoo. His smile was unchanged, but his attire suggested that fortune had not favored him lately.
Byomkesh welcomed Bikash warmly and said with a smile, “So, what news?”
Bikash replied, “Not good news, sir. I’ve lost my job, now I just wander about.”
Byomkesh’s face grew serious—“On what charge did you lose your job?”
Bikash said, “If I’d committed a crime, I’d have been hanged, sir. I lost my job because I didn’t commit any crime.”
“Hm. So what are you doing now?”
“Roaming around looking for work. I came to see if you might have something for me.”
Byomkesh thought for a moment and said, “Work—? Well, we’ll talk about work later. It’s already late, why don’t you have lunch here?”
A strained smile of gratitude flickered across Bikash’s face—“No sir, I have to return home at noon. If you have any work, I’ll come back later.”
Looking at Bikash’s face, it seemed as if some hungry loved one was waiting for him at home.
Byomkesh, thinking again, said, “I do have a job, and I need a sharp man like you for it. I need you to dig up someone’s secrets. Interested?”
Bikash pulled a notebook and pencil from his pocket—“Name?”
Byomkesh said, “Have you heard of Shiuli Majumdar?”
“Shiuli Majumdar? The singer?”
“Yes. Her father’s name is Dayalhari Majumdar, address 13/3, Ramtanu Lane, Shyambazar. I need you to gather every detail about their household.”
Writing it down, Bikash asked, “When do you need the information?”

Byomkesh replied, “It’s not a day’s work. You’ll have to collect information bit by bit, over many days. The past, the present, who comes and goes from the house, what is said—I want to know everything. Remember these two names: Anadi Halder and Prabhat. Whenever you learn anything, come and tell me.”
“Very well, I’ll take my leave then.” Tucking the notebook and pencil into his pocket, Bikash stood up.
Byomkesh handed him a hundred-rupee note and said, “Here, take a hundred rupees for now. You’ll get more when the job’s done.”
Bikash took the note and gazed at it for a moment, unmoving, then his eyes...
Byomkesh Samagra

He said, “Byomkesh Babu, you can tell when a man hasn’t eaten by looking at his face—can’t you? You guessed right, didn’t you?” With that, Bikash swiftly bent down, touched Byomkesh’s feet, and hurried out.
Byomkesh closed the door and gave a whimsical laugh. “Some money put to good use. Come, let’s not delay—let’s bathe and eat. Otherwise, who knows, another guest might arrive at any moment.”
chapters.summary: Kestobabu flees after revealing secrets. Byomkesh sends letters and hires a man, Bikash, for a task.

chapters.title: Putiram’s Pain
paragraphs: Thirteen
It was late afternoon when Putiram brought in the tea. I noticed his face looked drawn and pained.
I asked, “What’s wrong, Putiram?”
He replied, “The pain from my acidity has started again, Babu.”
Byomkesh said, “I’ll give you some medicine. Go lie down, you don’t have to cook for us this evening.”

For some days now, Putiram had been suffering from gastritis; pure gravel and tamarind seed powder no longer agreed with him. Byomkesh gave him a dose of ajwain water and, returning, I said, “Let’s send word downstairs and have our meal at the mess today.”
Byomkesh thought for a moment and said, “No, let’s eat out at a hotel tonight. Five hundred rupees came into our hands today—it’s only right that a barbarian’s wealth be squandered.”
I couldn’t agree with his lightheartedness. “Byomkesh, don’t mind me. When you realized that five hundred rupees was a bribe, was it right for you to take it?”
Byomkesh replied, “I could offer you many arguments in response, but I won’t. I needed the money, so I took it. I can’t chase wild buffaloes while starving at home.”
“But suppose—suppose in the end we find out that Nimai and Nitai are the murderers. What then? Will you hush it up because you took a bribe?”
“No, I won’t hush it up. I’ll hand them over myself—if the police want to catch them, that is. Remember, they paid me to investigate Anadi Haldar’s murder, not as a bribe.”
“If that’s so, then it’s a different matter.”
“Don’t worry, I won’t commit a sin for a bribe. If I intended to do wrong, I wouldn’t have settled for five hundred—I’d have made sure my own interests were well served.” Byomkesh smiled as he spoke.

I finished my tea and lit a cigarette. I was thinking perhaps there would be no more visitors this evening, when Prabhat arrived. He carried a bundle in his hand; his appearance betrayed that he was only recently recovered from illness—the signs of weakness still lingered in his eyes.
Byomkesh said, “Come in. How are you feeling now?”
Prabhat smiled shyly. “I’m well. I troubled you a lot the other day.”
“It was nothing. What’s that in your hand?”
“A little sweet. I was passing by Bheem Nag’s shop and thought I’d bring something.”

When he opened the bundle, we saw it was no small amount—a good twenty or twenty-five rupees’ worth of dense, syrupy sandesh. The other day, Byomkesh had helped him, refusing to take any fee for the doctor or the car fare, so Prabhat was now trying, with utmost politeness, to return the favor. Byomkesh exclaimed with delight, “Ah, this is heavenly! Ajit, can you guess whose face I saw first this morning?”
Adimriphu 485
I said, “As far as I recall, you saw my face, and I saw yours.”

“Then you understand—our faces are not ordinary.” He paused. “Anyway, it’s best to put the food away. It’s not wise to leave things out.” Byomkesh took the sandesh inside and, returning, asked, “Prabhatbabu, will you have some tea?”
“No, thank you, I’ve already had tea.” He glanced around the room. “Only you two live here, I suppose?”
Byomkesh replied, “The two present are the only ones here. My wife and son are in Patna at the moment.”
Prabhat’s eyes seemed to dance—“In Patna!”
Byomkesh said, “Yes, with all the commotion here, I’ve kept them away. You still haven’t forgotten Patna, have you?”
“Forget Patna!” Prabhat’s voice grew deep. “I’ve spent my whole life there. So many friends. Ishaq Saheb is there.”
“Ishaq Saheb?”

“My master. I used to work in his shop—he taught me the clerk’s trade, guided me by the hand. There’s no one like him, a man like a god. He’s old now… who knows who works in his shop these days… perhaps he works alone.” Prabhat sighed.
Byomkesh asked, “Which para in Patna does he live in?”

“He lives in the city. Everyone there knows him. I haven’t been that way since I left Patna. Byomkeshbabu, you go to Patna from time to time, don’t you? Next time you go, will you visit Ishaq Saheb? See how he’s doing—I long to see him.”
“I’ll certainly visit him. And what news from this side? How is Kestobabu?”
Prabhat said, “Kestobabu has left.”
“He’s left?”
“Yes. He couldn’t get along in my house. He and my mother quarreled day and night. Then, one day, he left on his own.”
“Well, that’s one burden off your shoulders. And Nripenbabu? Does he work in your shop now?”
“Yes.”
“What does he do?”
“There’s a lot of running around in a bookshop. You have to fetch books from other shops, go to the post office to send V.P. parcels. I used to do all that myself. Now Nripenbabu does it.”
“Good.”

Prabhat had been speaking with Byomkesh all this while, occasionally glancing at me; now he turned fully towards me and said, “Ajitbabu, perhaps you remember I said I would come to see you. I couldn’t, with all this trouble. I have a request.”
“What request? Tell me.”
“You must give me one of your novels. I’m a poor publisher, just started a new shop. Still, I’ll pay you what any other publisher would.”
Byomkesh Samagra

There is always a risk in giving your book to a new publisher; you never know when the red light will flash. Once, I was cheated by an unknown publisher. I hesitated and said, “Well, at the moment, I have nothing on hand—”
Byomkesh said, “Why not give him the novel you’re working on? Prabhatbabu, don’t worry, you’ll get Ajit’s book.”

Prabhat, encouraged, replied, “You can give it to me when your book is finished. Right now, my shop isn’t doing well; selling other people’s books on commission brings hardly any profit. If I have your blessings, I’ll expand my shop; I’ll work with all my might, I won’t let it go to waste.”
Byomkesh said, “That’s what I want to hear. At your age, one must have enthusiasm for work. Only then can you progress.”
With a beaming face, Prabhat took out his wallet from his pocket, drew out two notes, and placed them before me. I saw: two hundred rupees. Truly, whose face had I seen upon waking today!
Prabhat said, “Here’s an advance honorarium. I’ll bring the rest as soon as the book is finished.” He stood up.
I said, “Take a receipt.”
He replied, “No, no, let the receipt wait till I pay the full amount. I must go now, it’s already evening, and my shop hasn’t opened yet.”

When Prabhat left, we sat for a while, gazing at each other in wonder and delight. Then, tucking the notes into my pocket with affection, I said, “What a marvel! It’s like a monsoon downpour—one-hundred-rupee notes raining down incessantly!”
Byomkesh said, “Hmm. Can one ever bear so much happiness?”
At that moment, Batul appeared at the doorway. It was time again for his collection round. With reverence, he greeted us and said, “I’ve come to collect the subscription, sir.”
Byomkesh glanced at me and smiled. The meaning of his smile: in the business of life, there is not only income, but also expenditure.
Seating Batul, Byomkesh went to fetch the money. From the notes given by Kaminikanta, he took one and handed it to Batul. “Do you have change, Batul?”
“Yes, sir, I do.”
Batul drew out his waist pouch. It was quite plump; inside were coins of all kinds, as well as notes of various denominations. I even spotted a few one-hundred-rupee notes.
Batul calculated and returned the change, then tied the pouch back around his waist. There was no doubt that Batul’s business was a profitable one.
Byomkesh offered Batul a cigarette. “Batul, have you heard that Anadi Halder is dead?”
Batul didn’t raise his eyes; carefully lighting the cigarette, he said, “Yes, sir, I’ve heard.”
“Someone shot him.”
“Yes, sir. That’s the rumor.”
“You know a lot of news, Batul. Can’t you guess who did it?”

“There are lakhs and lakhs of people in Calcutta, sir. How can I guess who did it among so many? But I must say, he brought it upon himself. If he hadn’t stopped my subscription, he wouldn’t have lost his life so carelessly. I would have protected him.”
“Exactly! Is it wise to quarrel with a crocodile while living in the water? Anadi Halder made a grave mistake. Let that be. Batul, do you people rent out rifles?”
Adimriphu 487
"Yes, sir, I can give it."
"On what terms do you rent it out?"

"Sir, the rent is twenty-five rupees per day; you'll get the rifle and two cartridges. However, at the time of renting, you have to deposit three hundred rupees. When you return the rifle, I deduct the rent and give the rest back. Do you need one, sir?"
"No, not at the moment. I just wanted to know the rate. Tell me, Batul, on the night Anadi Halder was murdered, did you rent out a rifle to anyone?"
Batul stood up. "Sir, I cannot say that. If I tell one customer's business to another, that would be betrayal; our trade would not survive. Well then, I’ll take my leave. My respects."

Batul left, and by then evening had fallen. Byomkesh stretched out in the easy chair and, I think, dozed off. My mind wandered here and there, always circling back to the two hundred rupees. Since I had taken the money, I would have to finish the novel quickly. Yet I cannot write in haste; my pen only moves when my mind is calm and untroubled. I tried to think about the novel, but Nimai, Nitai, Prabhat, Batul—all of them kept peeking in and out of my thoughts.
After two hours, hunger began to gnaw at my stomach, so I said, "Come on, let’s go out now. I’ll pay for the hotel meal today."
Byomkesh replied, "Excellent, excellent."
